stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with abnormal uterine bleeding, underwent an endometrial biopsy (see report). Endometrial biopsy: Atypical complex hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Atypical hyperplasia is premalignant and is definitively treated by hysterectomy, but this patient is "25-year-old", so fertility should be preserved. The fertility-sparing treatment is progestogen therapy (oral progesterone) with close follow-up and repeat endometrial sampling.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tamoxifen has an estrogen-agonist effect on the endometrium and causes hyperplasia; it is never a treatment for it.
B. Hysterectomy is the treatment of atypical hyperplasia when childbearing is complete or in older/postmenopausal women; it would end fertility in a 25-year-old.
D. Endometrial ablation does not treat atypia, destroys fertility and hampers later endometrial surveillance.
key_concept:
Endometrial hyperplasia management depends on atypia and fertility wishes.
  • Without atypia: progestogen therapy
  • With atypia, family complete or older: total hysterectomy
  • With atypia, young or wants fertility: progestogen with follow-up biopsies
  • Diagnosis: endometrial biopsy
  • Risk factors: unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS, diabetes, tamoxifen)
exam_pearl: Same biopsy in a 50 or 57 year old flips the answer to hysterectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's short version (25 yrs female with atypical complex hyperplasia) highlights Progesterone; fuller Q version answer: C. Oral progesterone.

stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 26 weeks of gestation diagnosed with large genital warts in the vulva. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: In pregnancy (26 weeks) the deciding factor is fetal safety: cryotherapy is a physical ablative method with no systemic absorption, so it is safe at any gestation and is the key here. Most chemical and immunologic wart treatments are avoided in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Electrocautery (or surgical excision) is the usual choice for refractory or very bulky warts; it is not the marked answer here because cryotherapy is the simple, pregnancy safe first choice.
C. Podophyllin resin is antimitotic and is absorbed systemically; it is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic and toxic). It is an option only in non pregnant patients.
D. Intralesional interferon is not recommended in pregnancy and is reserved for refractory disease in non pregnant patients; it is not first line anywhere.
key_concept:
Genital warts in pregnancy: physical ablation, not chemicals.
  • Simple wart: cryotherapy (safe in pregnancy)
  • Refractory or large wart: electrocautery / surgical excision
  • Avoid in pregnancy: podophyllin, podophyllotoxin, interferon
  • Warts may grow in pregnancy and regress postpartum
exam_pearl: The word "pregnant" removes podophyllin and interferon at once; between the physical methods, the key goes to cryotherapy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed options: cryotherapy (highlighted), electrotherapy, podophylline resin, fluconazole. Screenshot also marks **A. Cryotherapy.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia for the last 8 months. She is known to be diabetic and hypertensive. Ultrasound: Thickened endometrial lining of approximately 23 mm. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
OptD: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
why_right: She is 45 with 8 months of menorrhagia, is diabetic and hypertensive (markers of chronic unopposed estrogen exposure), and has a markedly thickened endometrium of "23 mm". Abnormal uterine bleeding at 45 or older is itself an indication for endometrial sampling, and the concern is hyperplasia or carcinoma. Only an endometrial biopsy gives histology, so it has the highest diagnostic value.
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI cannot provide a tissue diagnosis; it is used for local staging once cancer is confirmed.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy views the peritoneal cavity and outside of the uterus (for example endometriosis) and cannot sample the endometrial cavity.
D. CT is for detecting distant spread and staging, not for diagnosing an endometrial lesion.
key_concept:
Who needs endometrial sampling in AUB.
  • AUB at age 45 or older
  • Under 45 with chronic unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS) or AUB failing medical treatment
  • Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrium >5 mm
  • Diabetes, hypertension and obesity raise hyperplasia and cancer risk
  • Imaging (MRI, CT) is for staging after histology
exam_pearl: "Highest diagnostic value" for an endometrial lesion means tissue; imaging only stages.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option A circled in pen; screenshot Answer: A.

stem: Folic acid dose for pregnant known case of sickle cell disease stable on remission?
why_right: Sickle cell disease causes chronic hemolysis, which depletes folate, so a pregnant woman with SCD needs high dose folic acid throughout pregnancy rather than the standard 0.4 mg. This recall's key is 2.4 mg because it is the only high dose option offered; the textbook high dose is about 4 to 5 mg daily.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0.2 mg is below even the routine preconception dose and is inadequate for any pregnancy.
B. 0.8 mg is close to the average risk dose (0.4 mg) used for women with no added risk; SCD needs a high dose because of ongoing hemolysis.
C. 1.4 mg is still well below the high dose range and is not a recognized regimen; the highest offered option is chosen instead.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose by NTD / folate risk:
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg daily, from at least 1 month before conception
  • High risk (previous NTD, SCD, antiepileptics, diabetes, obesity): high dose, 4 to 5 mg daily
  • SCD: continue high dose throughout pregnancy (hemolysis keeps consuming folate)
  • Hydroxyurea is stopped in pregnancy (teratogenic)
exam_pearl: If 5 mg is listed, pick it; if not, choose the highest dose offered for SCD.

stem: Female with irregular menstrual cycle, she is obese and BMI 31. Labs and blood test are pending.
why_right: An obese woman (BMI 31) with an irregular cycle and labs still pending most likely has a weight related ovulatory disorder such as PCOS. Lifestyle modification (diet and exercise for weight loss) is first line for every such patient: even modest weight loss can restore ovulation and regular cycles, and it is appropriate before any diagnosis is confirmed.
why_wrong_block: B. Combined OCP is the treatment for menstrual irregularity once PCOS is confirmed and pregnancy is not desired; it is added after or alongside lifestyle change, not chosen before workup is complete, and estrogen adds VTE risk in obesity.
key_concept:
PCOS / anovulation management ladder:
  • Step 1 for all: lifestyle modification and weight loss
  • Menstrual irregularity, no pregnancy wish: combined OCP
  • Infertility: ovulation induction (clomiphene or letrozole)
  • Insulin resistance: metformin
  • Hirsutism: OCP, then antiandrogen
exam_pearl: "Labs pending" plus obesity means start with lifestyle; OCP becomes the answer when PCOS is confirmed and the question asks for cycle control.

stem: bhCG Day 1: 1200 mIU/mL; Day 4: 1000 mIU/mL; Day 7: 800 mIU/mL; Day 14: 500. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptD: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
why_right: After methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy the decisive comparison is day 4 vs day 7: here 1000 falls to 800, a 20% decline (more than 15%), and it keeps falling to 500 by day 14. This is a successful response, so the plan is to repeat β-hCG weekly until it is undetectable.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceasing follow up is wrong while β-hCG is still 500; weekly levels must continue until undetectable to exclude persistent trophoblast.
B. Immediate surgery is for rising β-hCG between day 4 and day 7, rupture or hemodynamic instability; levels here are falling steadily.
D. A second methotrexate dose is for a plateau or a fall of less than 15% from day 4 to day 7; here the fall exceeds 15%.
key_concept:
Single dose methotrexate monitoring (compare day 4 with day 7):
  • Fall >15%: weekly β-hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second dose of methotrexate
  • Rising: surgical management
  • A rise from day 1 to day 4 is expected and not failure
  • Rupture or instability at any point: surgery
exam_pearl: Ignore day 1; only the day 4 to day 7 change decides between follow up, second dose and surgery.

stem: Pregnant with uncontrolled bleeding resulting in DIC. What is the most common cause?
why_right: Placental abruption is the most common cause of DIC in pregnancy. Retroplacental clot releases tissue factor (thromboplastin) into the maternal circulation, consuming clotting factors and platelets, so bleeding becomes uncontrolled; risk rises with severe or concealed abruption and fetal death.
why_wrong_block:
A. Placenta previa causes painless, often heavy bleeding, but it is a mechanical bleed from the lower segment and rarely triggers DIC.
C. A congenital bleeding disorder (for example von Willebrand disease) can cause pregnancy bleeding but is rare and is not a consumptive coagulopathy.
D. Uterine rupture causes pain, shock and loss of fetal station, usually with prior cesarean or uterotonics; it is far less common than abruption as a cause of DIC.
key_concept:
Obstetric causes of DIC:
  • Most common: placental abruption
  • Others: amniotic fluid embolism, severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP, sepsis, retained dead fetus, massive PPH
  • Abruption: painful bleeding, tender hard uterus, risk factors hypertension, smoking, trauma
  • Previa: painless bleeding, no vaginal exam
exam_pearl: "Pregnant + DIC" defaults to abruption; sudden collapse with hypoxia during labor points to amniotic fluid embolism instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: restatement (massive uncontrollable vaginal bleeding leading to coagulopathy) also highlights B. Placental abruption.

stem: Patient present with large leiomyoma and menorrhagia prolonged menstruation, see image Hb is 70 What is Most Appropriate Next management Step?
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to correct the anemia.
  • Severe anemia from fibroid bleeding: correct anemia first
  • Asymptomatic incidental fibroid: observe, yearly ultrasound
  • Symptomatic: medical first (OCP; GnRH agonist preoperatively to shrink)
  • Large (>7 cm) or failed medical: myomectomy (fertility) or hysterectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: When a low Hb is in the stem and "correct the anemia" is an option, it comes before any fibroid treatment.

Compiler note: No answer marked for this version. Next item (1566) is the same recall without the anemia option, marked OCP.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient present with large leiomyoma and menorrhagia prolonged menstruation, see image Hb is 70 What is Most Appropriate Next management Step?
why_right: This is the variant with no anemia correction option. Among what is offered, the source keys OCP as the next step because symptomatic fibroid bleeding is treated medically first, before uterine artery embolization or surgery, and hormonal control reduces menstrual loss while her anemia is managed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is the fertility sparing surgery for a large fibroid (above about 7 cm) or failed medical treatment; it is not the immediate step in a patient with Hb 70 who has not yet had medical treatment.
B. Uterine artery embolization is reserved for a surgical candidate who refuses surgery; it is not the first line next step.
C. This option is an empty placeholder in the recall; had it said "correct the anemia", that would be the answer (see the sister card).
key_concept:
Fibroid treatment ladder:
  • Severe anemia present: correct anemia first if offered
  • Medical: OCP for symptom control; GnRH agonist before surgery to shrink
  • Surgery for large (>7 cm) or failed medical: myomectomy (fertility) or hysterectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: Same stem, two keys: with an anemia option pick anemia correction; without it, pick medical treatment (OCP) before procedures.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant of 1565 where no anemia correction option is given.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is attending the clinic complaining of post-menopausal bleeding for the last 3 months. She was found to have a uterine fibroid of 5 cm in size, noted in a recent ultrasound. Upon review of the previous medical records, the ultrasound performed 5 years ago showed the same size and location of the fibroid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Any post-menopausal bleeding must be evaluated for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma by endometrial sampling. The fibroid has been the same size and location for 5 years, so it is unlikely to be the new source of bleeding and must not be blamed; a growing fibroid after menopause would instead raise concern for sarcoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is a fertility-sparing operation for a symptomatic fibroid in a woman who wants children; it is irrelevant at 60 and skips the cancer workup.
B. Hysterectomy may end up being the treatment once histology is known, but operating before tissue diagnosis skips the essential next step and assumes the stable fibroid is the cause.
C. Uterine artery embolization is for symptomatic fibroids in women who decline surgery; it does nothing to exclude endometrial malignancy.
key_concept:
Post-menopausal bleeding = endometrium until proven otherwise.
  • AUB over 45 years: endometrial biopsy
  • Post-menopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium on TVUS: biopsy
  • Stable fibroid on serial imaging: not the culprit
  • Enlarging fibroid after menopause: suspect leiomyosarcoma
exam_pearl: Do not let an old, unchanged fibroid distract you from sampling the endometrium.

stem: Pt had low risk and uncomplicated pregnancy comes for labor. Which of the following is the best intrapartum surveillance to ensure maternal and fetal wellbeing during labor?
OptA: Maternal pulse and blood pressure monitoring
OptC: Early identification of possible labor complications
OptD: Intermittent fetal heart monitoring as it's low risk
why_right: The stem stresses a low risk, uncomplicated pregnancy. For low risk labor, intermittent auscultation of the fetal heart is the recommended fetal surveillance: it is as safe for the baby as continuous CTG and avoids the extra interventions (operative delivery) that continuous monitoring brings without benefit. The question asks for the surveillance that ensures fetal and maternal wellbeing, and fetal heart assessment is the core of that.
why_wrong_block:
A. Maternal pulse and blood pressure are recorded in every labor but say nothing about fetal wellbeing. They become the focus when there is a maternal risk such as hemorrhage or preeclampsia.
B. Contractions are assessed during labor to judge progress, but contraction monitoring alone does not tell you whether the fetus is coping. It is paired with fetal heart assessment, not a substitute for it.
C. Early identification of complications is the goal of intrapartum surveillance, not a surveillance method. It describes why we monitor rather than how.
key_concept:
Fetal heart monitoring method follows risk.
  • Low risk, uncomplicated: intermittent auscultation
  • High risk (FGR/SGA, preeclampsia, diabetes, previous CS, meconium, oxytocin, epidural): continuous CTG
  • Abnormal heart rate on intermittent auscultation: switch to continuous CTG
exam_pearl: Low risk + 'best surveillance' = intermittent auscultation; continuous CTG in low risk labor adds interventions without improving outcome.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0963B).

stem: A 22-year-old, otherwise healthy woman, presents to the Emergency Room complaining of amenorrhea for the last 8 weeks and expelling blood and tissue through the vagina. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
OptD: Pelvic examination and CT scan of the pelvis
highlight_terms_source: expelling blood and tissue through the vagina
why_right: 8 weeks of amenorrhea with "expelling blood and tissue" means a miscarriage is under way, and the type is defined by two things: whether the cervical os is open or closed and what remains in the uterus. A pelvic (speculum and bimanual) examination assesses the os and any tissue at it, and ultrasound shows retained products or an empty cavity. Together they classify the miscarriage and guide management.
why_wrong_block:
B. Punch biopsy is used for visible cervical lesions and has no role in diagnosing a miscarriage.
C. Abdominal examination cannot assess whether the cervical os is open or tissue is at the os, which is what separates the miscarriage types.
D. CT is not used to evaluate an early pregnancy; it adds radiation and shows uterine contents less well than ultrasound.
key_concept:
Miscarriage type = os status (pelvic exam) + tissue status (ultrasound).
  • Open os, tissue partly passed: incomplete
  • Open os, tissue not passed: inevitable
  • Closed os, all tissue passed: complete
  • Closed os, tissue not passed, non-viable: missed
  • Closed os, viable fetus with bleeding: threatened
exam_pearl: The pelvic exam, not the abdominal exam, tells you if the os is open, which is the fork between miscarriage types.

stem: A 23-year-old primigravida presented at 31 weeks of gestation with preterm labor. Examination revealed, the uterus is contracting and the cervix is closed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is magnesium sulfate because at 31 weeks (below 32 weeks) a woman in preterm labor is given MgSO4 for fetal neuroprotection, reducing the risk of cerebral palsy if she delivers. The listed alternatives are tocolytics only and none of them protects the fetal brain. MgSO4 is not chosen for its tocolytic effect, which is weak and not recommended for that purpose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nifedipine is a first-line tocolytic that can buy time for steroids, but it gives no fetal neuroprotection, which this key prioritizes below 32 weeks.
B. Terbutaline is a beta mimetic with significant maternal side effects (tachycardia, pulmonary edema); it is not first line and has no neuroprotective effect.
C. Indomethacin is a tocolytic option before 32 weeks, but it risks fetal ductus constriction and oligohydramnios and gives no neuroprotection.
key_concept:
Preterm labor drug ladder by gestation.
  • Below 32 weeks: MgSO4 for neuroprotection
  • Below 34 weeks: antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity (priority if asked for a single drug)
  • Tocolysis (nifedipine, atosiban; indomethacin below 32 weeks) to allow steroids to work
  • GBS prophylaxis antibiotics if delivery expected
exam_pearl: If corticosteroids are among the options below 34 weeks, they take priority over MgSO4.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1969).

stem: A 27-year-old G3 P2 AO L2 at 34 weeks of gestation with severe preeclampsia. Which of the following is the rationale behind giving antihypertensive medications?
OptD: Decrease risk of maternal complications such as stroke
why_right: In "severe preeclampsia" severe-range BP is treated to protect the mother: uncontrolled hypertension causes hemorrhagic stroke, a leading cause of maternal death in preeclampsia. Antihypertensives do not change the placental disease, so they give no proven fetal benefit; delivery is the only cure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oligohydramnios reflects placental insufficiency; lowering maternal BP does not prevent it.
B. Fetal demise is driven by the underlying placental pathology, which antihypertensives do not reverse; the fetal answer is timely delivery.
C. Growth restriction is not reduced by antihypertensives; overly aggressive lowering may even reduce placental perfusion.
key_concept:
Severe preeclampsia management goals:
  • Antihypertensives → prevent maternal stroke
  • Magnesium sulfate → prevent eclamptic seizures
  • Delivery → definitive cure
  • Steroids if preterm → fetal lung maturity
exam_pearl: Antihypertensives in preeclampsia are for the mother's brain, not the baby.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with small for gestational age fetus and reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Antenatal steroids and delivery within 1 week
OptD: Repeat ultrasound growth assessment in 2 weeks
why_right: An SGA fetus with reversed end-diastolic flow (REDV) on umbilical artery Doppler at "33 weeks" is past the gestation at which REDV mandates delivery (32 weeks or more). Surveillance is no longer acceptable, but she is still preterm, so a course of antenatal corticosteroids is given where time allows and delivery is planned promptly afterwards. The key therefore pairs steroids with delivery rather than delivery without steroid cover.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weekly Doppler is routine surveillance for FGR with reassuring results; once REDV appears at 32 weeks or more, waiting a week risks fetal death.
B. Immediate caesarean without steroid cover gives up the neonatal lung benefit of steroids at 33 weeks while the fetus is not yet acutely compromised; immediate delivery is right if CTG or BPP is already abnormal.
D. A growth scan in 2 weeks ignores REDV, the most severe umbilical Doppler finding; growth interval scans suit SGA with normal Doppler.
key_concept:
Umbilical artery Doppler in FGR decides timing.
  • Normal: weekly surveillance, deliver at 37 weeks or more
  • AEDV: deliver at 34 weeks or more; earlier, daily testing
  • REDV: deliver at 32 weeks or more; earlier, daily testing
  • Abnormal CTG or BPP at any stage: deliver
  • Steroids before preterm delivery when time allows; caesarean usually preferred
exam_pearl: REDV below 32 weeks = daily surveillance with steroids; REDV at 32 weeks or more = deliver.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with small for gestational age fetus and reversed enddiastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Antenatal steroids and delivery within 72 Hours
OptD: Repeat ultrasound growth assessment in 2 weeks
why_right: An SGA fetus with reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler is the most severe Doppler finding before fetal decompensation, and at 33 weeks (≥32 weeks) the fetus should be delivered rather than monitored. Because she is still preterm (<34 weeks), a course of antenatal corticosteroids is given first to reduce neonatal respiratory distress, with delivery planned promptly afterwards. This recall's key combines both needs: steroids plus delivery within a short window.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weekly Doppler is the surveillance step for FGR with normal or reassuring studies; once REDV appears at ≥32 weeks, waiting a week risks intrauterine death.
B. Delivery is indicated, but at 33 weeks steroids are given first when the fetus is not in acute distress; immediate CS without steroids would be right with a non-reassuring CTG/BPP or maternal instability.
D. A growth scan in 2 weeks ignores the Doppler result; serial growth scans suit an SGA fetus with normal umbilical artery Doppler.
key_concept:
FGR management is driven by umbilical artery Doppler and gestational age.
  • Normal/reassuring: weekly UA Doppler, BPP, NST; deliver at ≥37 weeks
  • Absent EDV: deliver at ≥34 weeks; below that, daily testing
  • Reversed EDV: deliver at ≥32 weeks; below that, daily testing
  • Non-reassuring BPP/NST at any stage: deliver
  • Preterm delivery <34 weeks: give corticosteroids first if time allows
exam_pearl: REDV at ≥32 weeks means deliver, not repeat scanning; the only debate is whether to give steroids first or deliver immediately.

stem: A WOMAN IN 41 WEEKS IN LABOR WITH GUSH OF FLUID?
key_concept:
Name the rupture by gestation and by labor status.
  • SROM: rupture after labor contractions start (any gestation)
  • PROM: rupture before labor at ≥37 weeks
  • PPROM: rupture before labor at <37 weeks
  • Preterm labor: contractions with cervical change <37 weeks
  • Confirm ROM: sterile speculum pooling, nitrazine (alkaline), ferning
exam_pearl: The decisive point is the order of events: rupture after contractions start is spontaneous (SROM), rupture before contractions at term is PROM.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Following item 1654 (page 420) is a note only: If Before Contraction -> PROM; If After Contraction -> SROM. S-ROM = AFTER contraction (regardless of GA); P-ROM = BEFORE contraction (at 37 weeks and beyond); P-P-ROM = BEFORE contraction (<37 weeks).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 61-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distension, early satiety, weight loss, and pelvic discomfort. Investigations reveal markedly elevated CA-125 levels. Imaging and biopsy confirm high-grade epithelial ovarian carcinoma with extensive metastatic spread throughout the abdomen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and excision of visible metastases
OptB: Start chemotherapy, then reassess for surgery
highlight_terms_source: extensive metastatic spread throughout the abdomen
key_concept:
Advanced ovarian cancer: decide between surgery first and chemo first.
  • Fit + disease looks completely resectable: primary debulking, then adjuvant chemotherapy
  • Extensive disease unlikely to be fully removed, or unfit: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then interval debulking
  • Palliation only if unfit for any treatment
  • Radiotherapy is not standard
exam_pearl: Words like 'unresectable', 'poor surgical candidate' or 'extensive spread' push toward chemo first; plain 'advanced' alone usually keys to surgery first.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option marked on the numbered recall. The following 'Q:' (62-year-old, advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, surgery highlighted) is carded separately.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 62-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain, constipation and anorexia for 8 months. On examination, a solid irregular fixed pelvic mass was appreciated. Pelvic transvaginal ultrasonography showed a multilocular ovarian mass. Based on staging and histological classification, she was diagnosed with an advanced epithelial ovarian cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptA: Chemo then see if surgery possible
OptB: Surgery to remove all the cancer
why_right: She has advanced epithelial ovarian cancer diagnosed by staging and histology, with no statement that she is unfit or the disease is unresectable. The mainstay is surgery to remove all visible cancer (cytoreduction: hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy and debulking), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. The amount of residual disease after surgery is the main driver of survival.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemo first then reassess (neoadjuvant chemotherapy) is chosen when complete removal looks unlikely or she is too unfit for major surgery; neither is stated here.
C. Radiotherapy is not a standard line of management in ovarian cancer, which spreads across the peritoneal cavity.
D. Palliative care only would deny effective treatment; advanced ovarian cancer still responds well to surgery plus chemotherapy, and palliation alone is for patients unfit for any therapy.
key_concept:
Advanced epithelial ovarian cancer:
  • Workup: TVUS, then CA-125; CT or MRI to plan
  • Staging is surgical
  • Treatment: maximal cytoreductive surgery, then adjuvant chemotherapy
  • Surgery alone is incomplete in advanced disease
  • Neoadjuvant chemo only if unresectable or unfit
exam_pearl: Surgery plus chemo is the pair: if 'surgery followed by chemotherapy' appears it beats 'surgery' alone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 1687.

stem: Patient diagnosed with ectopic pregnancy measuring 4 cm. Most appropriate treatment?
why_right: The decisive clue is the size: an ectopic mass of 4 cm fails the methotrexate size criterion (mass must be under 4 cm). Methotrexate needs every criterion to be met, so a mass of 4 cm or more is managed surgically, usually by laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy.
why_wrong_block: A. Methotrexate is right only when ALL criteria are met: hemodynamically stable, beta-hCG ≤5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass under 4 cm and a compliant patient for follow up; the 4 cm mass fails here.
key_concept:
Ectopic pregnancy: medical vs surgical.
  • Methotrexate needs ALL: stable, beta-hCG ≤5000 IU/L, no cardiac activity, mass under 4 cm, reliable follow up
  • Surgery if: unstable or ruptured, mass ≥4 cm, any MTX contraindication, or failed MTX
  • Laparoscopy preferred over laparotomy
  • Salpingostomy needs serial beta-hCG follow up (risk of persistent trophoblast)
exam_pearl: One failed criterion (size, hCG, cardiac activity or instability) is enough to move the answer from methotrexate to surgery.

stem: Dysmenorrhea with nodularity on uterosacral ligament.
why_right: Dysmenorrhea with nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments is the classic examination finding of endometriosis (deep implants in the pouch of Douglas). The fuller version adds a fixed retroverted uterus and infertility, completing the picture of the 3 Ds plus subfertility.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adenomyosis (adenomyoma) gives dysmenorrhea and heavy bleeding with a uniformly enlarged, boggy, tender uterus, typically in an older multiparous woman; it does not produce uterosacral nodules.
C. Leiomyoma causes heavy menstrual bleeding with an enlarged, irregular, firm uterus; the nodularity is on the uterus itself, not the uterosacral ligaments.
key_concept:
Endometriosis:
  • Symptoms: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, plus infertility and chronic pelvic pain
  • Exam: normal sized, fixed retroverted uterus with tender uterosacral nodularity
  • Initial test: TVUS (endometrioma with ground glass appearance)
  • Confirmatory test: laparoscopy with biopsy
  • Adenomyosis: enlarged boggy uterus; fibroids: enlarged irregular uterus
exam_pearl: Uterosacral nodules point outside the uterus (endometriosis); an enlarged uterus points inside it (adenomyosis or fibroids).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version: 24-year-old nulliparous with cyclic debilitating pelvic pain, heavy menses, trying to conceive; immobile retroverted uterus with nodularity and tenderness of uterosacral ligaments; **C. Endometriosis marked.

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 29 weeks of gestation presented with preterm labor. Which of the following tocolytics can cause patent ductus arteriosus?
why_right: Indomethacin is an NSAID (prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor). Prostaglandins keep the fetal ductus arteriosus open, so indomethacin is the tocolytic with ductus arteriosus effects: in utero it causes premature ductal constriction (with fetal pulmonary hypertension), and it also causes oligohydramnios. It is therefore limited to short courses before 32 weeks; disturbed ductal closure after birth has also been reported.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atosiban is an oxytocin receptor antagonist with few maternal or fetal side effects and no ductal effect.
B. Ritodrine is a beta mimetic; its effects are maternal (tachycardia, palpitations, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema), not ductal.
C. Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker; side effects are maternal hypotension, flushing, headache and reflex tachycardia, not ductal.
key_concept:
Any question linking a tocolytic to the fetal ductus arteriosus points to indomethacin.
  • Indomethacin: ductal constriction, oligohydramnios; avoid after 32 weeks
  • Beta mimetics: maternal tachycardia, pulmonary edema
  • Nifedipine: hypotension, headache, flushing
  • Atosiban: best tolerated
exam_pearl: Indomethacin closes the ductus in utero (and is used to close a PDA in neonates); prostaglandin E1 keeps it open.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall (options Ritodrine, Nifedipine, Indomethacin) highlights Indomethacin; 'Q:' version Answer: D (GB). Note: indomethacin classically causes premature closure of the ductus; answer as marked.

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy had an ultrasound confirming Monochorionic Monoamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
why_right: In monozygotic twins the membranes depend on when the embryo splits. By days 9 to 12 the chorion and the amnion have both already formed, so the twins share one chorion and one amniotic sac: monochorionic monoamniotic.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0-72 hours: split before the chorion forms, so each twin gets its own chorion and amnion (dichorionic diamniotic).
B. 4-8 days: chorion already formed but not the amnion, giving monochorionic diamniotic twins (the most common monozygotic type).
D. >12 days: the embryonic disc has begun to form, so splitting this late is incomplete and produces conjoined twins.
key_concept:
Monozygotic cleavage timing:
  • 0-3 days (0-72 hours): Di Di
  • 4-8 days: Mono Di
  • 9-12 days: Mono Mono
  • 13 days or later: conjoined
  • Dizygotic twins are always Di Di
exam_pearl: The later the split, the more is shared: chorion first, then amnion, then the body itself.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2393).
Compiler note: Original recall: "monochorionic monoamniotic ..day of cleavage"; compiler supplied the fuller "Q:" version.

stem: Pregnant woman at 14 weeks. Mother is O negative, father Rh positive. Previous pregnancy history present. Current pregnancy shows no anti-D antibodies. Most appropriate management?
why_right: She is Rh negative with an Rh positive partner and the current pregnancy shows "no anti-D antibodies", so she is unsensitized and needs prevention, not surveillance. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks, then again within 72 hours after delivery if the baby is Rh positive. At 14 weeks with no sensitizing event, nothing extra is due yet.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-D now: at 14 weeks it is given only after a sensitizing event (vaginal bleeding, miscarriage, abdominal trauma, amniocentesis/CVS); none is described, so wait for the routine 28 week dose.
C. MCA Doppler: screens for fetal anemia in an already sensitized pregnancy (positive antibody titer); she has no antibodies, so there is no fetal anemia to look for.
D. No intervention: an Rh negative mother with an Rh positive partner is at risk of alloimmunization; omitting prophylaxis risks hemolytic disease in this or future pregnancies.
key_concept:
Rh negative mother: antibody screen decides the pathway.
  • Antibody negative (unsensitized): anti-D at 28 weeks + within 72 h postpartum if baby Rh positive
  • Any sensitizing event (bleeding, trauma, procedures, miscarriage): extra anti-D at that time
  • Antibody positive (sensitized): anti-D is useless; serial titers, then MCA Doppler for fetal anemia
exam_pearl: Anti-D prevents sensitization; once antibodies are present, switch to surveillance (titers, MCA Doppler), never prophylaxis.

stem: Woman with 4 cm ectopic pregnancy in the right fallopian tube scheduled for surgery. Most appropriate management?
why_right: A 4 cm tubal ectopic fails the methotrexate size criterion (mass must be under 4 cm), so surgery is indicated, and at surgery the standard procedure is salpingectomy of the affected (right) tube. Salpingectomy removes all trophoblast and needs only a single postoperative beta hCG to confirm the fall.
why_wrong_block:
B. Remove both tubes: there is no indication to remove a healthy contralateral tube; bilateral salpingectomy is chosen only when the other tube is diseased, e.g. a left hydrosalpinx in an IVF patient.
C. Methotrexate during surgery: not a routine adjunct; single dose methotrexate is used after salpingostomy if beta hCG plateaus or rises (persistent trophoblast).
key_concept:
Tubal ectopic at surgery: salpingectomy vs salpingostomy.
  • Salpingectomy (default, normal contralateral tube): one beta hCG to confirm drop
  • Salpingostomy (tube preserved, e.g. contralateral tube damaged and fertility wanted): serial beta hCG
  • Plateau or rise after salpingostomy: single dose methotrexate
  • MTX criteria: stable, hCG ≤5000, no cardiac activity, mass <4 cm, compliant
exam_pearl: Remove both tubes only if the opposite tube is also diseased (hydrosalpinx before IVF); otherwise take only the affected tube.

stem: Pregnant came to the antenatal clinic with history of 2 preterm delivery, and now she is having vaginal spotting, what to give now? (Only this without details)
why_right: Two previous preterm deliveries place her in the highest risk group for recurrent spontaneous preterm birth, and progesterone supplementation is the drug used to reduce that risk; it also supports the pregnancy when she presents with vaginal spotting. The recall gives only this context and two hormones, and progesterone is the pregnancy-maintaining hormone.
why_wrong_block: A. Estrogen: has no role in preventing preterm birth or treating bleeding in pregnancy; estrogen is used for problems like atrophic vaginitis or hormone replacement, not in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Prior spontaneous preterm birth: prevention tools.
  • Vaginal progesterone from the second trimester (IM 17-OHPC was withdrawn in the US in 2023)
  • Serial transvaginal cervical length; short cervix may need cerclage
  • History-indicated cerclage if recurrent second trimester losses suggest cervical insufficiency
  • Active preterm labor <34 weeks is different: steroids, tocolysis, MgSO4 if <32 weeks
exam_pearl: Progesterone prevents preterm birth in a high risk woman; it is not a tocolytic and does not stop established labor.

stem: A 30-year-old 12 weeks pregnant woman presented to the Emergency Room with vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed her fundal height is consistent with 19 weeks (see report). Ultrasound: Findings are consistent with molar pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach in management?
highlight_terms_source: fundal height is consistent with 19 weeks
why_right: First-trimester bleeding with a uterus larger than dates (19 weeks at 12 weeks) and ultrasound consistent with molar pregnancy is a hydatidiform mole. Treatment is suction evacuation, which empties the large soft uterus completely with less perforation and bleeding risk, followed by serial beta-hCG surveillance. It also preserves fertility in this 30-year-old.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate is for post-molar GTN (beta-hCG plateau or rise after evacuation), not first-line treatment of the mole itself.
B. Hysterectomy is an option only for a woman who has completed childbearing (and does not remove the need for hCG follow-up); this young patient needs fertility-sparing evacuation.
D. Sharp curettage carries a higher risk of perforation and incomplete evacuation in a soft, enlarged molar uterus; suction evacuation is the standard.
key_concept:
Molar pregnancy: suction evacuation, then beta-hCG surveillance.
  • Clues: bleeding, size greater than dates, hyperemesis, vesicles, snowstorm US
  • Baseline hCG, then repeat after evacuation
  • Weekly until undetectable, then monthly follow-up
  • Plateau or rising hCG: oncology for staging and chemotherapy
  • Follow-up is by hCG, not serial ultrasound
exam_pearl: Mole is evacuated by suction, not sharp D&C; methotrexate only enters if hCG fails to fall.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: "Molar pregnancy asked about its management: A. suction B. dilation curettage". Compiler's Q: Molar pregnancy Tx, A: suction & Evacuation. Screenshot (0337) Answer: C.

stem: Another Q about pregnant female in 3rd trimester All her previous BP f/u were normal 120/70 Now in this visit her BP is 160/100 No protein in urine No symptoms at all What is this
why_right: This recall's key is preeclampsia: a new 160/100 in the third trimester, after all previous readings were 120/70, is a severe-range reading, and the recall treats this abrupt severe hypertension as preeclampsia. Severe-range hypertension in pregnancy (≥160 systolic or ≥110 diastolic) is managed the same way as preeclampsia with severe features, which is the logic behind the key.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gestational HTN: new BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; the recall did not key it, treating the severe-range reading as the deciding feature (see concern).
C. Eclampsia: requires new-onset tonic-clonic seizures on a background of preeclampsia; she has no symptoms at all.
D. Chronic HTN: hypertension before 20 weeks or before pregnancy; all her previous readings were 120/70.
key_concept:
Hypertension in pregnancy: timing + proteinuria/end-organ signs decide.
  • Before 20 weeks or pre-pregnancy: chronic HTN
  • After 20 weeks, no proteinuria, no end-organ signs: gestational HTN
  • After 20 weeks + proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction (low platelets, high LFTs, renal, pulmonary edema, headache/visual): preeclampsia
  • Preeclampsia + seizures: eclampsia
  • Chronic HTN + new proteinuria/end-organ signs: superimposed preeclampsia
exam_pearl: Severe-range BP (≥160/110) in pregnancy is handled like preeclampsia with severe features: urgent antihypertensive treatment and delivery planning.

stem: A 39-year-old primigravida attended her routine prenatal visit at 39 weeks' gestation. She denied any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain. Urinalysis was negative for protein (see lab results). Vital signs at this visit: Blood pressure 160/90 mmH, Heart rate 84 /min Vitals signs at all other visits: Blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, Heart rate 68 /min Test Result Normal Values HCT 0.34 0.37-0.48 Platelets count 165 150-400 x 109/L Alanine aminotransferase 12 5-40 IU/L Aspartate aminotransferase 22 12-40 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: She has new hypertension at 39 weeks (160/90, with BP 120/70 at all previous visits), but urinalysis is negative for protein, she denies headache, visual change or abdominal pain, and platelets and liver enzymes are normal. New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction is gestational hypertension; the severe-range systolic makes it severe gestational hypertension, not preeclampsia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Eclampsia: requires new-onset convulsive seizures with preeclampsia; she has no seizures or symptoms.
B. Chronic hypertension: onset before 20 weeks or before pregnancy; all her earlier visits were normotensive.
D. Superimposed preeclampsia: needs pre-existing chronic hypertension plus new proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; she has neither.
key_concept:
Classify by onset and target organ signs.
  • <20 weeks or pre-pregnancy: chronic HTN
  • >20 weeks, no proteinuria, normal labs, no symptoms: gestational HTN
  • >20 weeks + proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction: preeclampsia
  • + seizures: eclampsia
  • Hb/HCT slightly low is not an end-organ criterion; check platelets, LFTs, creatinine, symptoms
exam_pearl: Normal platelets and LFTs with negative protein keep it gestational hypertension even when systolic hits 160.

stem: Young lady with secondary amenorrhea Had D&C 3 month ago, what is the investigation:
OptC: hystroscopy to look for intra-uterine adhesions
key_concept:
Secondary amenorrhea: let the history pick the test.
  • Always first: pregnancy test
  • Then TSH, prolactin, FSH
  • High prolactin, galactorrhea, visual signs: MRI brain
  • Recent D&C or uterine surgery, normal hormones, no withdrawal bleed: hysteroscopy (Asherman)
  • Ovarian cycle intact in Asherman, so premenstrual symptoms persist
exam_pearl: The history picks the test: recent uterine instrumentation raises intrauterine adhesions, while galactorrhea or high prolactin points to the pituitary.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with severe generalized abdominal pain, associated with nausea and vomiting for the last few hours. She is known to have an intrauterine contraceptive device inserted for the last 3 years. She did a home pregnancy test, which was positive. Ultrasound: Fluid collection of approximately 13 x 15 cm. No identified gestational sac. Both ovaries are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Fluid collection of approximately 13 x 15 cm
why_right: A positive pregnancy test with no gestational sac in the uterus means ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, and pregnancy occurring with an IUD in situ is more likely to be ectopic. The severe generalized abdominal pain with a large 13 x 15 cm fluid collection (hemoperitoneum) indicates that it has ruptured.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ruptured corpus luteum: can cause hemoperitoneum, but it would not explain a positive pregnancy test with an empty uterus, and both ovaries are reported normal.
B. Intact ectopic pregnancy: presents with mild localized pain, an adnexal mass and little or no free fluid; it would not produce a 13 x 15 cm collection or generalized pain.
key_concept:
Positive hCG + empty uterus: decide intact vs ruptured.
  • Intact: mild pain, adnexal mass, no or minimal free fluid, stable
  • Ruptured: severe pain, shoulder tip pain, peritonism, large free fluid in pouch of Douglas, possible shock
  • Ruptured or unstable: surgery, never methotrexate
  • Pregnancy with IUD in place: suspect ectopic
exam_pearl: Large free fluid on ultrasound converts an ectopic from intact to ruptured and mandates surgery.

stem: A 33-year-old pregnant woman G3P2 at 24 weeks' gestation presents to the clinic complaining of sudden, watery vaginal discharge. A sterile speculum examination is performed to evaluate for preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM). Which of the following proteins in the vaginal secretions can help establish the diagnosis of membrane rupture?
why_right: When sterile speculum findings (pooling, nitrazine, ferning) are equivocal, PAMG-1 is a protein abundant in amniotic fluid but present only in trace amounts in cervicovaginal secretions, so detecting it in vaginal fluid supports membrane rupture. It is the basis of a commercial bedside immunoassay used to confirm suspected PPROM, as in this 24 week woman with sudden watery discharge.
why_wrong_block:
A. Placental Protein 14 (PP14): also called glycodelin, an endometrial/decidual glycoprotein involved in implantation; it is not used to diagnose rupture of membranes.
C. Placental vasopressinase: a placental enzyme that degrades ADH and causes transient diabetes insipidus of pregnancy; it has no role in diagnosing PPROM.
D. Placental growth factor: an angiogenic marker that is low in preeclampsia (used with sFlt-1 to predict or rule out preeclampsia), not a marker of amniotic fluid leak.
key_concept:
Confirming rupture of membranes.
  • First: sterile speculum exam (pooling in posterior fornix); avoid digital exam
  • Bedside adjuncts: nitrazine (alkaline pH), ferning on microscopy
  • Protein immunoassays for equivocal cases: PAMG-1, IGFBP-1
  • Ultrasound: reduced amniotic fluid supports but does not prove rupture
exam_pearl: Placental growth factor sounds like a placental test for PPROM but belongs to preeclampsia screening; PAMG-1 is the amniotic fluid protein.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Short recall version: PPROM which protein could help establish the diagnosis? with B- Placental alpha-1 microglobulin 1 (PAMG-1) highlighted. Fuller version: Answer: B.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a leiomyoma associated with heavy menstruation she doesn't want children soon (see image Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
why_right: Symptomatic fibroids with heavy menstruation are treated medically first, and surgery is reserved for large fibroids or failure of medical treatment. Because she doesn't want children soon, combined oral contraceptive pills fit well: they reduce menstrual blood loss and provide contraception, while leaving future fertility intact.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy: fertility-sparing surgery for a woman who wants future pregnancy, with a large fibroid or failed medical therapy; not the first step before medical treatment is tried.
B. Hysterectomy: definitive surgery for a woman who has completed her family and failed or declined other treatment; she is 35 and may want children later.
D. Uterine artery embolization: an alternative for a surgical candidate who refuses surgery; not first line, and it may affect future fertility.
key_concept:
Fibroid management ladder.
  • Asymptomatic incidental: observe, annual ultrasound
  • Symptomatic (heavy bleeding): medical first, OCP (GnRH agonist pre-op to shrink)
  • Severe anemia: correct the anemia first
  • Large fibroid or failed medical: surgery
  • Wants fertility: myomectomy (submucosal: hysteroscopic); family complete: hysterectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a very low hemoglobin, the next step flips to correcting the anemia before treating the fibroid.

stem: 30-year-old G4 P3 at 30 weeks of gestation presents with severe pain in the right flank radiating to her groin. She also complains of rigors and chills. Urine analysis: Numerous pus cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: right flank radiating to her groin
why_right: "Severe pain in the right flank radiating to her groin" with "rigors and chills" and "numerous pus cells" in the urine is an upper urinary tract infection: pyelonephritis. Pregnancy predisposes to it through progesterone-related ureteric dilatation and stasis, and it is more often right-sided because the uterus rotates to the right and compresses the right ureter.
why_wrong_block:
A. Appendicitis in pregnancy causes right-sided abdominal pain (displaced upward), not loin pain radiating to the groin with marked pyuria and rigors.
C. Meckel's diverticulum typically presents in children with painless rectal bleeding, obstruction or diverticulitis, not flank pain with pyuria.
D. Round ligament pain is sharp groin or lower abdominal pain with movement, without fever, rigors or pyuria.
key_concept:
Flank pain + fever/rigors + pyuria in pregnancy = pyelonephritis.
  • Right side more common (dextrorotation of uterus)
  • Admit, IV antibiotics, hydration
  • Risks: preterm labor, sepsis, ARDS
  • Screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria to prevent it
exam_pearl: Rigors plus pus cells in the urine move the answer from surgical abdomen to pyelonephritis.

stem: Management of cervical cancer stage 2B:
why_right: This recall's key is radical hysterectomy: for invasive cervical cancer, an operation must remove the uterus together with the parametria and upper vagina, usually with pelvic lymphadenectomy. Stage 2B means parametrial invasion, and of the three surgical options offered only a radical hysterectomy removes the parametrium; conization and simple hysterectomy leave it behind.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conization: for microinvasive disease (stage IA1) when fertility is wanted, or as a diagnostic excision; far too limited for parametrial disease.
C. Other type of hysterectomy: simple (extrafascial) hysterectomy is for stage IA1 without fertility wish; it does not remove the parametria, so it is inadequate for invasive disease beyond that.
key_concept:
Cervical cancer treatment by stage.
  • IA1: conization (fertility) or simple hysterectomy
  • IA2 to early IB / IIA1: radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymph nodes (or chemoradiation)
  • IIB and above (parametrial or beyond): concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin + external beam + brachytherapy)
  • Fertility wish in early stage: radical trachelectomy
exam_pearl: Conization and simple hysterectomy are only for microinvasive (IA1) disease; anything more invasive needs the parametria addressed.

stem: Missed abortion how Tx ? It Was Infected Abortus , She Had Missed Abortion + Fever
key_concept:
Missed abortion management depends on stability and infection.
  • Stable, no infection, first trimester: expectant management
  • Stable, no infection, wants faster resolution: misoprostol (medical) or suction evacuation
  • Fever, foul discharge, uterine tenderness = septic abortion: IV broad spectrum antibiotics plus prompt evacuation
  • Surgical (suction) evacuation is preferred when infected, bleeding heavily or unstable
  • Methotrexate is for ectopic pregnancy, not intrauterine loss
exam_pearl: The word FEVER converts a missed abortion into a septic one: antibiotics are mandatory and evacuation cannot wait.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 14yr delayed 1ry amenorrhea + Cyclic pelvic pain on exam there is blue mass in vagina
why_right: A girl with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain and a bluish bulging mass at the vaginal introitus has menstrual blood trapped behind an imperforate hymen (hematocolpos). She is menstruating normally (cyclic pain shows ovulatory cycles) but the outflow is blocked at the lowest level, so the dark blood shows through the thin membrane.
why_wrong_block: B. Transverse vaginal septum also causes outflow obstruction with cyclic pain, but the block is higher in the vagina, so no bulging blue membrane is seen at the introitus; the hymen is normal and a blind vaginal pouch is found.
key_concept:
Primary amenorrhea with normal secondary sex characteristics and cyclic pain = outflow tract obstruction.
  • Imperforate hymen: bulging bluish membrane at the introitus; treat with hymenotomy (cruciate incision)
  • Transverse vaginal septum: no bulge at introitus, short blind vagina, septum higher up
  • Mullerian agenesis (MRKH): absent uterus, so NO cyclic pain; short blind vagina
  • Androgen insensitivity: absent uterus, scant pubic and axillary hair, XY
exam_pearl: Blue bulge AT the introitus = hymen; blind vagina with no bulge = septum or agenesis (cyclic pain points to septum).

stem: Couple w/ infertility Male good Female: B/L tubal block Management?
why_right: With a normal male factor and bilateral tubal blockage, the eggs cannot meet sperm through either tube, so the treatment is IVF, which bypasses the tubes entirely. Ovulation induction is pointless when both tubes are blocked.
why_wrong_block:
B. Induction with clomiphene is used for ovulatory dysfunction, or for confirmed UNILATERAL tubal blockage where one tube is still patent; here both tubes are blocked.
C. Ovulation induction with any agent fails for the same reason: ovulation is not the problem, the tubes are.
D. The recalled text is garbled ("No laparoscopy"). Laparoscopy with dye test is the step that CONFIRMS an abnormal HSG and is right if the block was seen only on HSG; once bilateral blockage is established, IVF beats tubal surgery.
key_concept:
Infertility ladder: semen analysis first, then ovulation, then tubes.
  • HSG = initial tubal test
  • Abnormal HSG: confirm with diagnostic laparoscopy and dye test
  • Confirmed unilateral block: ovulation induction (clomiphene)
  • Confirmed bilateral block: IVF
  • High prolactin: bromocriptine; anovulation (PCOS): letrozole or clomiphene
exam_pearl: HSG only showing a block: next step is laparoscopy and dye; already confirmed bilateral block: IVF.

stem: Women just delivered her baby and 30 min later after baby delivery the placenta did not come out, what to do?
why_right: The placenta is still undelivered 30 minutes after the baby, which defines a retained placenta. The next step is manual removal of the placenta under adequate analgesia or anesthesia with antibiotic cover; if tissue remains or removal fails, proceed to curettage.
why_wrong_block:
B. Waiting 30 minutes has already happened; that is the right step only before the 30 minute mark in a woman who is not bleeding heavily.
C. IV oxytocin is the first line drug for atonic bleeding (and is part of active management of the third stage), but once the placenta is retained beyond 30 minutes it does not replace removal of the placenta.
key_concept:
Third stage of labor = delivery of the placenta.
  • Up to 30 minutes: wait (with active management)
  • Not delivered at 30 minutes: manual removal under anesthesia plus antibiotics
  • Manual removal fails or retained tissue: dilatation and curettage
  • No cleavage plane: suspect placenta accreta
exam_pearl: Retained placenta with heavy bleeding does not mean waiting the full 30 minutes: bleeding brings manual removal forward.

stem: A women in her 30s gets her period every 45 day, and recently her period stopped for 6 months. What is the most likely cause:
why_right: This recall's key is hypothyroidism: in the original question the labs showed a high TSH, normal FSH and LH, and a raised prolactin. Hypothyroidism raises TRH, which stimulates prolactin, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility, giving oligomenorrhea (cycles every 45 days) that progresses to amenorrhea. The high prolactin is secondary, not a separate disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypopituitarism gives LOW FSH and LH (and low or inappropriately normal TSH with low thyroxine); in the source question the gonadotropins were normal and TSH was high.
C. PCOS also causes oligomenorrhea then amenorrhea, and would be favoured if hirsutism, acne or polycystic ovaries were given with normal TSH; a high TSH points to the thyroid instead.
D. Hyperprolactinemia is present but secondary to hypothyroidism (TRH drives prolactin); treat the thyroid and prolactin normalizes. Primary hyperprolactinemia would be the answer only with a normal TSH.
key_concept:
Secondary amenorrhea: first exclude pregnancy, then check TSH, prolactin, FSH and LH.
  • High TSH with raised prolactin: hypothyroidism (treat with levothyroxine)
  • Very high prolactin, normal TSH: prolactinoma (dopamine agonist, pituitary MRI)
  • Low FSH and LH: hypothalamic or pituitary cause
  • High FSH: premature ovarian insufficiency
  • Normal labs with hyperandrogenism: PCOS
exam_pearl: High prolactin WITH high TSH: the thyroid is the cause; always check TSH before labelling hyperprolactinemia.

stem: A pregnant woman with preeclampsia has just delivered and has a lax uterus with moderate postpartum hemorrhage. Physical examination reveals no laceration or retained product of conception. Which of the following medical therapies is most recommended?
OptD: 20 units oxytocin in a 500 mL of D5W given intravenously
why_right: "Lax uterus" with no laceration or retained tissue means atonic PPH, and first-line uterotonic is oxytocin by IV infusion (20 units in 500 mL fits the usual dose range). The decisive clue is "preeclampsia": ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, which removes both ergometrine options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin is a peptide inactivated in the gut, so it is never given orally; it is given IV or IM.
B. Ergometrine causes vasoconstriction and BP surges, so it is contraindicated in preeclampsia whatever the route; it would be a second-line option in a normotensive woman.
C. IM ergometrine has the same contraindication in hypertension; changing route or dose does not make it safe here.
key_concept:
Atonic PPH: massage + uterotonics.
  • 1st: oxytocin IV infusion
  • Ergometrine: avoid in hypertension/preeclampsia
  • Carboprost (PGF2α): avoid in asthma
  • Misoprostol, tranexamic acid as adjuncts
  • Failure → balloon tamponade, then surgery
exam_pearl: Preeclampsia + PPH: oxytocin yes, ergometrine no.

stem: A 25-year-old primigravida presents at 15 weeks of gestation to the antenatal visit where blood and urine investigations were requested. Which of the following is the most expected finding?
why_right: Total blood volume starts rising from about 6 weeks and reaches roughly 40 to 45% above baseline near term (plateau around 32 to 34 weeks). The question asks for the "most expected finding" of normal pregnancy physiology, and the 40 to 45% blood volume rise is the textbook figure (at 15 weeks it is still climbing toward it). Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, which causes the dilutional fall in hematocrit.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hematocrit falls in pregnancy because of hemodilution; it does not rise.
B. The direction is right but the size is wrong: hematocrit falls only modestly (physiological dilutional anemia). The 40 to 45% figure belongs to blood volume.
C. This underestimates the rise; total blood volume increases by about 40 to 45%, not 20 to 25%.
key_concept:
Pregnancy expands plasma more than red cells.
  • Blood volume: up 40 to 45% (peak 32 to 34 weeks)
  • Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass
  • Hematocrit: falls modestly (dilutional, physiological anemia)
  • GFR rises, so creatinine and urea fall
exam_pearl: 40 to 45% is the blood volume rise; any option giving a 40 to 45% change in hematocrit is the trap.

stem: A 23-year-old woman primigravida presents at 27 weeks' gestation with vaginal bleeding. She undergoes a transvaginal ultrasound showing a placenta previa. Which of the following is the most likely associated feature?
OptD: Profuse first episode of vaginal bleeding
why_right: In placenta previa the placenta sits over the cervix, so any contact or contraction, such as intercourse, can disrupt its attachment and cause bleeding. Postcoital spotting in pregnancy is therefore a classic associated feature and should raise suspicion of previa in this 27-week primigravida.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulopathy (DIC) is the classic complication of placental abruption with concealed bleeding, not of previa.
B. Previa bleeding is characteristically painless; painful bleeding with a tender uterus points to abruption.
D. The first (sentinel) previa bleed is usually small and stops spontaneously; heavy bleeding tends to come with later episodes.
key_concept:
Antepartum hemorrhage by pain and timing:
  • Painless bleeding: placenta previa (soft, non-tender uterus)
  • Painful bleeding, tender uterus: abruption (DIC risk)
  • Painless bleeding at rupture of membranes with fetal distress: vasa previa
  • Previa risk factors: prior cesarean, multiple gestation
exam_pearl: Previa = painless, small sentinel bleed, postcoital spotting; abruption = pain, tenderness, DIC.

stem: A 35-year-old G3 P2002 woman presents to the clinic near term. Ultrasound demonstrates that the fetal head is in the fundus, the fetal spine is parallel to the mother's spine, with extended knees and flexed hips. Both arms are flexed at the elbows. Which of the following is the most appropriate description of fetal presentation?
highlight_terms_source: fetal head is in the fundus
why_right: "Fetal head is in the fundus" with the spine parallel to the mother's means a longitudinal lie with breech presentation. The breech subtype is defined by the legs: "extended knees and flexed hips" (feet up by the face) is a frank breech. The flexed arms do not change the classification.
why_wrong_block:
B. Complete breech has BOTH hips and knees flexed (fetus sits cross legged); here the knees are extended.
C. Compound presentation means a limb (usually a hand) prolapses alongside the presenting part; it is not defined by hip and knee posture, and the arms here are simply flexed.
D. Incomplete (footling) breech has one or both hips extended so a foot or knee is lowermost; here both hips are flexed.
key_concept:
Breech subtype = hips and knees.
  • Frank: hips flexed, knees extended (most common at term)
  • Complete: hips flexed, knees flexed
  • Incomplete/footling: hip(s) extended, foot or knee lowermost
  • Lie = fetal long axis vs maternal; presentation = part over the inlet
exam_pearl: Frank breech: flexed hips + extended knees; add flexed knees and it becomes complete.

stem: A 60-year-old menopausal woman presents with recent on-and-off vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most common cause of her complaint?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding, and that is endometrial atrophy from estrogen deficiency: the thin, fragile endometrium bleeds intermittently ("on and off"). Cancer is the cause you must exclude, but it is not the most frequent.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometrial cancer is the most important cause to exclude with TVUS and sampling, but it accounts for only a minority of postmenopausal bleeding; pick it when risk factors (obesity, diabetes, nulliparity) or a bulky uterus are given.
B. Polyps are a recognized cause but less common than atrophy.
D. Fibroids regress after menopause and rarely cause postmenopausal bleeding.
key_concept:
Postmenopausal bleeding: two different questions.
  • Most common cause: atrophy
  • Most important to exclude: endometrial cancer
  • Workup: TVUS endometrial thickness, then endometrial biopsy if thickened or persistent
  • Obese, diabetic, hypertensive, bulky uterus: think cancer
exam_pearl: Read the verb: most COMMON = atrophy, most likely with risk factors or most serious = cancer.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is complaining of heavy menstruation lasting for 14 days every period. She is morbidly obese and has type 2 diabetes mellitus (see lab results and report). Ultrasound: Endometrial thickness of 18 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
why_right: She is "46-year-old" with prolonged heavy bleeding ("14 days"), "morbidly obese" with "type 2 diabetes" (unopposed estrogen risk) and an "18 mm" endometrium. AUB over 45 years, or with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, requires endometrial tissue; an office (pipelle) endometrial sample is the next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pelvic CT: gives no histology of the endometrium; used for staging once cancer is confirmed.
B. Pelvic MRI: assesses local extent (myometrial invasion) after a tissue diagnosis; it is not the first diagnostic step.
C. Hysteroscopy: right when office sampling is inadequate, nondiagnostic, or bleeding persists, or when a focal lesion such as a polyp is suspected. Office sampling comes first.
key_concept:
Endometrial sampling indications in AUB:
  • Age over 45 with AUB
  • Younger with risk factors: obesity, diabetes, PCOS, chronic anovulation, tamoxifen, failed medical therapy
  • Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrium >4 to 5 mm
  • Office biopsy first; hysteroscopy if inadequate or focal lesion
  • CT/MRI only for staging after diagnosis
exam_pearl: Obesity and diabetes in a perimenopausal woman with AUB mean biopsy now, not imaging.

stem: A 20-year-old woman came to the clinic for prenatal care. She missed her period for the last 6-8 weeks. Home pregnancy test was positive 2 weeks back and negative before that. Her periods were irregular and she is unsure of the last day of her menstrual period. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for dating her
OptC: Wait 3-4 weeks then do an ultrasound
OptD: Counting from the positive urine pregnancy test
highlight_terms_source: unsure of the last day of her menstrual period
why_right: Her dates are unreliable ("periods were irregular", "unsure of the last day"), so pregnancy must be dated by ultrasound. At an estimated 6 to 8 weeks, an early transvaginal scan measuring the crown-rump length is the most accurate dating method, and accuracy falls the later it is done, so the scan should be done now.
why_wrong_block:
B. Quantitative hCG confirms pregnancy and is used to follow early pregnancy or pregnancy of unknown location, but values vary too widely to date a pregnancy.
C. Waiting gains nothing; first-trimester crown-rump length is the most accurate dating parameter, so delaying only reduces precision.
D. The date a home test turned positive reflects when she happened to test, not conception or the LMP, so it cannot date the pregnancy.
key_concept:
Uncertain LMP or irregular cycles: date the pregnancy by early ultrasound.
  • First trimester dating parameter: crown-rump length (most accurate)
  • Certain LMP with regular cycles: Naegele rule, confirmed by dating scan
  • hCG: confirms pregnancy and tracks viability, does not date it
exam_pearl: Unsure dates means ultrasound now; never wait and never count from the pregnancy test.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presented with mild pelvic pain and spotting. She was diagnosed with an ectopic pregnancy and offered medical management. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to treat this patient?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the drug used when an ectopic pregnancy is "offered medical management". Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that stops the rapidly dividing trophoblast, so the ectopic resolves without surgery. It is used only in a stable patient with mild symptoms ("mild pelvic pain and spotting") who meets the selection criteria and can attend serial beta-hCG follow-up.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin is a uterotonic for induction/augmentation of labour and atonic postpartum haemorrhage; it has no effect on trophoblast outside the uterus.
B. Carboprost (PGF2 alpha) is a second-line uterotonic for atonic PPH and is avoided in asthma; it does not treat ectopic pregnancy.
C. Misoprostol (PGE1) is used for medical management of missed or incomplete miscarriage, cervical ripening and PPH; it expels intrauterine tissue, not a tubal pregnancy.
key_concept:
Ectopic pregnancy: stable and meets criteria = methotrexate; unstable or ruptured = surgery.
  • MTX needs: haemodynamically stable, unruptured
  • beta-hCG ≤5000 IU/L
  • No embryonic cardiac activity
  • Mass <4 cm
  • Compliant with serial beta-hCG follow-up
exam_pearl: Shock, rupture, fetal cardiac activity or a mass ≥4 cm flips the answer from methotrexate to surgery.

stem: A 31-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 had an uneventful pregnancy and went into spontaneous vaginal delivery. She delivered a healthy boy weighing 3000 g. After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in managing this patient?
OptA: Start blood transfusion with O negative blood
OptB: Send blood tests and manage accordingly
OptC: Take her to the operating room for surgical management
OptD: Call for help and make sure there is cross-matched bloop
why_right: Heavy bleeding right after placental delivery is primary postpartum hemorrhage, most often from uterine atony. The lead in asks for the initial step: PPH is a team emergency, so you call for help and ensure cross matched blood is available while checking uterine tone and starting massage and uterotonics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Uncrossmatched O negative blood is reserved for massive hemorrhage with instability when cross matched blood is not yet available; nothing here says she is in shock.
B. Sending blood tests and waiting for results delays resuscitation; labs are drawn in parallel, not as the first management step.
C. Surgery comes only after failed medical treatment (uterotonics) and balloon tamponade; it is not the initial step.
key_concept:
PPH after vaginal delivery: escalate stepwise.
  • Call for help, two large bore lines, cross match blood
  • Check uterine tone; if boggy: bimanual massage plus uterotonics
  • Uterotonics: oxytocin first; methylergonovine (avoid in hypertension); carboprost (avoid in asthma); misoprostol
  • Next: Bakri balloon; then embolization if stable or surgery if unstable
  • Last: hysterectomy
exam_pearl: 'Initial step' in PPH is the call for help and blood; 'best drug' is oxytocin (or the only uterotonic listed).

stem: U.S.P.T.F., what is the most appropriate gestational age to screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria? (Another wording: "in what trimester is asymptomatic bacteriuria screening indicated according uspstf guidlines")
why_right: Pregnant women are screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria with a urine culture at the first antenatal visit; USPSTF places this at 12 to 16 weeks (or the first visit if later), i.e. late first trimester. 12 weeks is the only option in that window, and if asked for the trimester the answer is the first. Screening early allows treatment before bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis, preterm labor or low birth weight.
why_wrong_block:
B. 20 weeks is the time of the anomaly scan and cervical length screening, not bacteriuria screening; it is too late to be the recommended window.
C. 26 weeks falls in the 24 to 28 week window for gestational diabetes screening, not bacteriuria.
D. 30 weeks is third trimester; bacteriuria is treated if found then, but screening is not timed there.
key_concept:
Match the screening test to its week.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria (urine culture): 12 to 16 weeks or first visit
  • Dating ultrasound: first trimester (about 10 to 13 weeks)
  • Anomaly scan: 18 to 22 weeks
  • GDM screening (low risk): 24 to 28 weeks
  • GBS swab: 36 to 37 weeks
exam_pearl: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is screened and treated ONLY in pregnancy (and before urologic procedures), never in other healthy adults.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Room with mild vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 9 weeks ago. Examination revealed the uterus is palpable, soft, and reaching to just above the symphysis pubis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
OptD: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
highlight_terms_source: last menstrual period was 9 weeks ago
why_right: An 18-year-old with a period "9 weeks ago", mild vaginal bleeding and a "soft" uterus palpable just above the symphysis is most likely pregnant with first-trimester bleeding. Pelvic ultrasound confirms an intrauterine pregnancy, gives gestational age and viability, and looks for the cause of bleeding (miscarriage, molar pregnancy, ectopic).
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal X-ray: exposes the fetus to radiation and gives no information about the pregnancy; it fits bowel obstruction or perforation.
B. MRI of the pelvis: not a first-line test in early pregnancy bleeding; reserved for problem solving such as placenta accreta or complex masses.
D. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis: a staging study (for example metastatic choriocarcinoma after a diagnosis), not an initial test, and carries high radiation dose.
key_concept:
First-trimester bleeding: confirm pregnancy, then ultrasound (transvaginal preferred).
  • Uterus first palpable just above the symphysis at about 12 weeks
  • Uterus larger than dates: think molar pregnancy, twins, wrong dates, fibroids
  • Ultrasound answers location, viability and dating at once
exam_pearl: Pregnancy suspected plus bleeding: the investigation is ultrasound; any option with radiation is a distractor.

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida who is Rh-negative delivered an Rh-positive infant. She received routine prophylactic Rh immunoglobulin at 28 weeks of gestation. What dose of anti-D immunoglobulin should she receive after delivery?
why_right: An Rh-negative mother who "delivered an Rh-positive infant" needs postpartum anti-D within 72 hours, even after the routine 28-week dose. The standard dose is 300 (printed as mg; the true unit is micrograms), which neutralizes about 30 mL of fetal whole blood.
why_wrong_block:
B. 1000 is not a standard dose; extra anti-D is given only when a quantified fetomaternal hemorrhage exceeds what 300 micrograms covers.
C. 2000 is not a standard dose; larger amounts are calculated from a measured fetomaternal hemorrhage, not given routinely.
D. The 28-week prophylaxis does not replace the postpartum dose; it would only be unnecessary if the baby were Rh-negative or she were already sensitized.
key_concept:
Anti-D prophylaxis in an unsensitized Rh-negative mother.
  • Routine dose at 28 weeks
  • Postpartum dose within 72 hours if the baby is Rh-positive
  • After any sensitizing event: bleeding, trauma, amniocentesis
  • 300 micrograms covers about 30 mL fetal whole blood
  • Larger bleed: quantify (e.g. Kleihauer-Betke) and give extra
exam_pearl: Antenatal anti-D at 28 weeks does not cancel the postpartum dose for an Rh-positive baby.

stem: A 23-year-old woman, a known case of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, delivered at 39 weeks of gestation, and her delivery was complicated with postpartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: In a known case of ITP the bleeding problem is a low platelet count, so active bleeding (PPH) is treated by replacing platelets with platelet transfusion, given regardless of the count and combined with steroids or IVIG to raise the count.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen (and factor VIII); it is used when fibrinogen is low, as in obstetric DIC after abruption, not in ITP.
B. Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors (raised PT/INR, as in liver disease or warfarin); ITP has normal coagulation factors.
C. Packed red cells restore oxygen carrying capacity in major blood loss but do not correct the platelet defect causing the bleeding.
key_concept:
Match the blood product to the defect.
  • Low platelets (ITP) + bleeding: platelets, plus steroids or IVIG
  • Low clotting factors, high INR: FFP (or PCC)
  • Low fibrinogen (DIC, abruption): cryoprecipitate
  • Anemia / massive loss: packed red cells
exam_pearl: ITP with active bleeding gets platelets even though transfused platelets are destroyed; abruption with DIC gets cryoprecipitate.

stem: A 33-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation presented with vaginal itching, burning, and irritation. Examination revealed a thick discharge with the appearance of cottage cheese in the vagina. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: thick discharge with the appearance of cottage cheese
why_right: Itching, burning and a thick cottage cheese discharge are vulvovaginal candidiasis. Because she is pregnant (36 weeks), treatment is a topical azole (for example clotrimazole or miconazole) given as a longer course, since oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral fluconazole is first line outside pregnancy but is avoided in pregnancy because of possible fetal risk.
B. Topical antivirals treat genital herpes, which gives painful vesicles and ulcers rather than curdy discharge.
C. Topical estrogen treats atrophic vaginitis in postmenopausal women (thin pale mucosa, little discharge), not a fungal infection.
key_concept:
Vaginal discharge by appearance:
  • Cottage cheese, itchy, odorless: Candida, azole (topical in pregnancy)
  • Thin grey, fishy, clue cells: bacterial vaginosis, metronidazole
  • Frothy yellow green, strawberry cervix: Trichomonas, metronidazole
  • Dry, thin mucosa, postmenopausal: atrophic vaginitis, topical estrogen
exam_pearl: Same picture in a non pregnant woman: oral fluconazole becomes acceptable; pregnancy flips it to topical only.

stem: A newly married woman is presented to the gynecology clinic for a routine examination and checkup. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
why_right: In a routine gynecological examination, the pelvic digital (bimanual) examination gives the most diagnostic information because it directly assesses the cervix, uterine size, position, mobility and tenderness, and the adnexa. A newly married woman is sexually active, so a digital vaginal examination is appropriate.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vaginal inspection: shows only visible surfaces (vulva, vagina, cervix) and cannot assess the size, mobility or tenderness of the pelvic organs.
B. General appearance: non-specific and of low diagnostic value for pelvic pathology.
C. Abdominal examination: detects only large pelvic masses that rise into the abdomen; it cannot evaluate the cervix, uterus and adnexa in detail.
key_concept:
Highest diagnostic value in a routine gynecological exam = pelvic digital (bimanual) examination.
