  • Bimanual: cervix, uterine size/position/mobility, adnexal masses, tenderness
  • Exception: painless antepartum bleeding: ultrasound BEFORE any digital exam (placenta previa)
  • Virgin patient: avoid digital vaginal exam; use rectal exam or ultrasound
exam_pearl: The 'newly married' clue tells you a digital vaginal exam is acceptable; in a virgin it would not be.

stem: A 30-year-old G5P4 woman presents in labor at 37 weeks of gestation. Examination revealed the cervix is found to be 10 cm dilated and the vertex is at -3 station. Cardiotocography shows that the baseline is 90 beats per minute, accelerations were present, good variability with recurrent late decelerations present. The uterine contractions are regular and strong, occurring at a rate of 4 in 10 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: The CTG shows baseline 90 bpm (bradycardia) with recurrent late decelerations: this is fetal distress even though accelerations and variability are preserved. Fetal distress requires expedited delivery, and although the cervix is 10 cm, the vertex is at -3 station, so vaginal assisted delivery is not possible. Emergency cesarean section is the fastest safe route.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin increases contraction stress on an already compromised fetus and is contraindicated in fetal distress; contractions are already strong at 4 in 10.
B. Full dilatation alone is not enough; instrumental delivery needs the head at +2 or lower. It would be right with the same CTG and the head at +2 or +3.
D. Reassurance fits a reassuring CTG; leaving a bradycardic fetus with late decelerations risks hypoxic injury.
key_concept:
Fetal distress: the delivery route is decided by dilatation and station.
  • Fully dilated + head at +2 or lower: instrumental delivery
  • Fully dilated but head high (above +2): cesarean
  • Not fully dilated: cesarean
  • Never augment with oxytocin when the CTG is non-reassuring
exam_pearl: 10 cm tempts you toward forceps; the -3 station is what forces cesarean.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida presents in labor at 37 weeks of gestation. Examination revealed the cervix is found to be 10 cm dilated and the head is at +3 station. Cardiotocography shows that the baseline is 120 beats per minute, accelerations were present, good variability, and a prolonged deceleration was noted for the last 7 minutes. The uterine contractions are regular and strong. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A prolonged deceleration for 7 minutes means the fetus needs expedited delivery. She is in the second stage with the cervix 10 cm and the head at +3 station, which meets the criteria for instrumental delivery (full dilatation, head at +2 or lower). Ventouse or forceps delivers faster than a cesarean at this point.
why_wrong_block:
A. A prolonged deceleration of this length is not reassuring; observation would be right only for a reassuring CTG.
B. Contractions are already regular and strong, and oxytocin would worsen fetal compromise; it is for inadequate contractions with a reassuring CTG.
D. Cesarean is the route when the head is high or the cervix is not fully dilated; with the head at +3 and full dilatation, instrumental delivery is quicker.
key_concept:
Expediting delivery for fetal compromise: match the route to the station.
  • Full dilatation + head at +2 or lower: ventouse or forceps
  • Head above +2 or cervix not fully dilated: emergency cesarean
  • Prolonged deceleration or persistent bradycardia in the second stage with a low head: instrumental delivery
exam_pearl: Fetal distress does not always mean cesarean; a low head at full dilatation means instrumental delivery.

stem: A 40-year-old G8P7 woman presents in active labor at 40 weeks of gestation. Examination revealed the cervix was found to be 7 cm dilated. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 120 beats per minute, no decelerations, and poor variability with recurrent variable decelerations. The uterine contractions are regular and strong, occurring at a rate of 4 in 10 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: poor variability with recurrent variable decelerations
why_right: At 7 cm she is in the active phase, and the CTG shows poor variability with recurrent variable decelerations, a non-reassuring tracing that signals fetal distress. Fetal distress calls for expedited delivery, and since she is not fully dilated, the route is emergency cesarean section. Contractions are already strong (4 in 10), so there is nothing to correct on the power side.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin would increase contraction stress and worsen fetal distress; contractions are already adequate.
B. Forceps need full dilatation and the head at +2 or lower; she is only 7 cm.
D. Reassurance fits a reassuring CTG; with poor variability and recurrent decelerations it leaves the fetus at risk of hypoxia.
key_concept:
Non-reassuring CTG in the first stage: stop or avoid oxytocin, resuscitate in utero, deliver by cesarean if not resolving.
  • Steps: maternal left lateral position, IV fluids, stop oxytocin, tocolysis if hyperstimulation
  • Not fully dilated: cesarean
  • Fully dilated + head at +2 or lower: instrumental delivery
exam_pearl: The stem contradicts itself ("no decelerations" then "recurrent variable decelerations"); poor variability with recurrent decelerations is the decisive clue.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presented to the clinic with prolonged and heavy menstruation for the last 8 months. She underwent an endometrial biopsy. Endometrial biopsy: Presence of endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: "Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia" is a premalignant lesion with a high risk of progression to, or coexisting, endometrial cancer. In a "50-year-old" with no fertility wish, the definitive management is total hysterectomy (bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is added in postmenopausal women and individualized if still premenopausal). Progestogen is kept for women who want fertility or are unfit for surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Chemotherapy is not used for a premalignant lesion; it is reserved for advanced or metastatic endometrial cancer.
C. Radiotherapy treats established endometrial cancer (adjuvant or primary when inoperable), not atypical hyperplasia.
D. Progesterone is first line for hyperplasia without atypia, or for atypia only when fertility is desired or surgery is impossible; neither applies at 50.
key_concept:
Atypical hyperplasia: hysterectomy unless fertility wish or unfit for surgery.
  • Atypia + childbearing complete/age ~50: hysterectomy
  • Atypia + young, wants fertility: oral progestogen with close follow-up
  • Atypia + unfit for surgery: continuous progestogen
  • No atypia: progestogen
exam_pearl: The word "atypia" plus no fertility wish flips the answer from progesterone to hysterectomy.

stem: A 45-year-old otherwise healthy woman presents to the clinic complaining of amenorrhea for the last 18 weeks. Her periods prior to this were all regular. Ultrasound: Presence of a snowstorm pattern within the uterine cavity. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to reach the diagnosis?
why_right: A "snowstorm pattern" filling the uterine cavity after 18 weeks of amenorrhea is the classic ultrasound picture of a complete hydatidiform mole. Molar pregnancy is diagnosed by ultrasound plus serum beta-hCG, which is markedly elevated (often 50,000 to 100,000 IU/L) because the trophoblast overproduces it. hCG is also the tumor marker used to monitor for persistent trophoblastic disease after evacuation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Alpha-fetoprotein is the marker for neural tube defects, yolk sac tumor and hepatocellular carcinoma, not trophoblastic disease.
C. CA 125 is raised in epithelial ovarian cancer (and benign pelvic conditions); a snowstorm uterus is not an ovarian process.
D. CEA is a marker for colorectal and other gastrointestinal or mucinous tumors and has no role in molar pregnancy.
key_concept:
Trophoblastic disease marker = beta-hCG.
  • Complete mole: snowstorm US, uterus large for dates, very high hCG
  • Diagnosis: ultrasound plus serum beta-hCG
  • Follow-up after evacuation: serial hCG until normal
  • AFP: NTD, yolk sac tumor, HCC
  • CA 125: epithelial ovarian cancer
  • CEA: colorectal and GI tumors
exam_pearl: Age 45 does not exclude a mole; older maternal age is actually a risk factor for complete mole.

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida presented at 34 weeks of gestation with eclamptic seizures. The seizures were controlled, and her blood pressure was brought down by antihypertensive medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Eclampsia is an indication for delivery at any gestation once the mother is stabilized. Her seizures are controlled and BP is lowered, so the stabilization steps are complete and the next step is to arrange delivery now; the risk of further seizures and maternal complications persists until delivery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation is expectant management, which is contraindicated after eclampsia.
B. Discharge is unsafe; eclampsia needs inpatient stabilization and delivery.
C. Prolonging pregnancy to 37 weeks is not acceptable in eclampsia; waiting to term applies only to gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia without severe features.
key_concept:
Eclampsia: ABC, then MgSO4, then BP control, then deliver.
  • Delivery after stabilization, regardless of gestation
  • Mode: induction is usually possible; cesarean for obstetric indications
  • Severe pre-eclampsia ≥34 weeks: stabilize, MgSO4, deliver
  • Pre-eclampsia without severe features: deliver at 37 weeks
exam_pearl: 'Arrange for delivery' does not mean crash cesarean before stabilization: stabilize first, then deliver.

stem: A 42-year-old P3003 healthy woman presents with heavy prolonged vaginal bleeding over the past 7 months. Her periods have become longer and progressively heavier, with the last one occurring 15 days ago. Pelvic examination reveals a small amount of blood in the vaginal vault, normal-sized uterus, and mobile ovaries. (See reports.) Pelvic ultrasound: Endometrium 13 mm and a 2.2 cm x 1 cm lesion in the uterine cavity. Endometrial biopsy: Normal histology. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Magnetic resonance imaging of the uterus
OptD: Evaluate hemoglobin level and coagulopathy screening
highlight_terms_source: 2.2 cm x 1 cm lesion in the uterine cavity
why_right: Ultrasound shows a focal 2.2 x 1 cm intracavitary lesion, but the blind endometrial biopsy was normal. A biopsy samples only part of the cavity and can miss a focal lesion, so the lesion must still be characterized: saline infusion sonohysterogram outlines polyps versus submucous fibroids and guides hysteroscopic removal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Examination under anesthesia does not image the uterine cavity; it is used for assessing pelvic or cervical pathology, not a focal intracavitary lesion.
C. MRI is costly and not first line for a focal cavity lesion; it is reserved for mapping complex fibroids or suspected adenomyosis when ultrasound is inconclusive.
D. Coagulation screening is for heavy bleeding since menarche or without a structural cause; here a structural lesion has already been found in a healthy woman.
key_concept:
Normal blind biopsy does not exclude a focal intracavitary lesion.
  • AUB >45 yr: endometrial biopsy
  • Focal lesion on TVUS: sonohysterogram
  • Then hysteroscopy for diagnosis and removal
  • Coagulopathy screen: heavy bleeding since menarche, no structural cause
exam_pearl: Focal lesion on US + normal biopsy = sonohysterogram, not reassurance.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1993).

stem: A 39-year-old woman presented with heavy menorrhagia and pelvic pressure with Lower limb heaviness and edema. Pelvic ultrasound confirms the presence of uterine fibroid. What is the most likely location of this fibroid?
why_right: This recall's key is Intramural because the picture combines heavy menorrhagia with bulk effects: pelvic pressure and lower limb heaviness and edema, which suggest a large fibroid compressing pelvic veins. Intramural fibroids sit in the muscle wall, enlarge the uterus and the endometrial surface, so they can produce both heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical fibroids are rare; they cause local pressure effects (urinary or bowel symptoms, obstructed labor) rather than heavy menstrual bleeding.
B. Subserosal fibroids grow outward and cause pressure or heaviness but typically NOT menorrhagia, so they do not explain her bleeding.
D. Submucosal fibroids are the classic cause of menorrhagia and infertility; pick them when bleeding dominates without marked bulk symptoms such as leg edema.
key_concept:
Fibroid location by symptom.
  • Submucosal: menorrhagia, infertility, (pressure)
  • Intramural: bulky uterus, pressure, can increase bleeding
  • Subserosal: pressure/heaviness, little bleeding
  • Cervical: rare, urinary/bowel symptoms, obstructed labor
  • Ultrasound is the initial and diagnostic test
exam_pearl: Menorrhagia alone = submucosal; menorrhagia plus large-mass pressure effects (leg edema) is how this recall points to intramural.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0520).

stem: A 20-year-old woman presented with a history of primary infertility for 1 year. She had a history of scanty irregular cycles with prolonged intervals (see lab results). Which of the following is the important workup?
why_right: The labs are not reproduced in this recall, but the intended picture is premature ovarian insufficiency: a 20-year-old with scanty, irregular, widely spaced cycles and labs showing high FSH and LH with low estradiol. Ovarian failure this young needs a karyotype to look for Turner mosaicism or another chromosomal cause, which also guides counselling and screening.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pelvic imaging does not reveal the chromosomal cause of ovarian insufficiency; MRI would be chosen for a structural pelvic question.
B. TSH is part of a general oligomenorrhea screen, but with an ovarian failure lab pattern the important test is karyotype.
C. Hyperprolactinemia gives low or normal FSH/LH, not the high gonadotropins of ovarian failure; choose prolactin if galactorrhea or low gonadotropins are shown.
key_concept:
Read the gonadotropins in oligo/amenorrhea:
  • High FSH/LH, low estradiol, young: ovarian insufficiency, karyotype
  • Low or normal FSH/LH + high prolactin: hyperprolactinemia, then pituitary MRI
  • LH:FSH raised, androgens high: PCOS
  • Always exclude pregnancy and check TSH
exam_pearl: Young woman with high FSH = karyotype; low FSH with high prolactin = pituitary.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1995).
Compiler note: Lab results referenced in stem are not shown on the page.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is complaining of severe abdominal pain. She is a known case of primary infertility and underwent embryo transfer 3 weeks ago (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: She had "embryo transfer 3 weeks ago" for infertility and now has "severe abdominal pain"; the labs would show a positive beta hCG. Assisted reproduction (IVF, embryo transfer) and the tubal disease that often underlies infertility are recognised risk factors for ectopic (including heterotopic) pregnancy. Pregnancy plus severe pain after IVF is ectopic until proven otherwise.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ovarian torsion: ovarian stimulation can enlarge the ovaries and predispose to torsion, so it is a real differential, but a positive pregnancy test after embryo transfer with severe pain points first to ectopic. Torsion fits sudden unilateral pain with vomiting and an adnexal mass.
C. Acute appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with fever and anorexia; it has no link to embryo transfer and does not explain a positive hCG.
D. Intestinal obstruction: colicky pain with vomiting, distension and absolute constipation, usually after prior surgery or hernia; nothing in this stem suggests it.
key_concept:
Severe abdominal pain in early pregnancy: exclude ectopic first.
  • Risk factors: IVF/embryo transfer, previous ectopic, PID or tubal surgery, IUD in situ, smoking
  • IVF also raises risk of heterotopic pregnancy (intrauterine + ectopic)
  • Work up: beta hCG + transvaginal ultrasound
  • Unstable: surgery; stable and small: methotrexate or expectant per criteria
exam_pearl: An intrauterine pregnancy on scan after IVF does not fully exclude ectopic: heterotopic pregnancy is more likely after assisted reproduction.

stem: A 36-year-old G4 P3003 is admitted in preterm labor at 36+5 weeks with polyhydramnios. Fetal bradycardia is noted after spontaneous rupture of membranes. Which of the following needs to be excluded by a prompt vaginal examination?
why_right: "Polyhydramnios" with "spontaneous rupture of membranes" allows a gush of fluid to carry the cord below the presenting part, and sudden "fetal bradycardia" right after ROM is the classic sign of cord compression from cord prolapse. A prompt vaginal examination confirms it (cord felt in the vagina) and lets you elevate the presenting part while arranging immediate delivery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Breech is a risk factor for cord prolapse but does not itself cause acute bradycardia; presentation is checked by abdominal exam or ultrasound.
C. Abruption (also triggered by sudden decompression of polyhydramnios) presents with pain, a tense tender uterus and bleeding; it is a clinical diagnosis and vaginal examination does not exclude it.
D. Arm prolapse occurs with transverse lie and causes obstructed labor rather than abrupt bradycardia; the emergency that compresses fetal blood flow is the cord.
key_concept:
Bradycardia immediately after ROM = cord prolapse until proven otherwise.
  • Risk factors: polyhydramnios, malpresentation, prematurity, multiparity, high presenting part
  • Diagnose: vaginal exam (or cord visible at the introitus)
  • Act: call for help, elevate presenting part (manual or bladder filling), knee chest or left lateral position
  • Deliver urgently: CS, or instrumental if fully dilated
  • Avoid handling the cord (vasospasm)
exam_pearl: Bradycardia after ROM with no bleeding = cord prolapse; with painful bleeding and a tender uterus = abruption.

stem: A 36-year-old presented to the Antenatal Clinic for an Ultrasound scan. Ultrasound: Single viable fetus with significant increased levels of amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: Polyhydramnios results from either reduced fetal swallowing or increased fetal urine output. In anencephaly the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid normally, so fluid accumulates. It is the only option that raises fluid; the other three all cause oligohydramnios.
why_wrong_block:
B. Post-term pregnancy is linked to declining placental function and oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios.
C. Posterior urethral valves obstruct fetal urine outflow, reducing amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios).
D. Maternal NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin) reduce fetal renal output and cause oligohydramnios; indomethacin is even used therapeutically to reduce fluid.
key_concept:
Polyhydramnios = fetus cannot swallow, or makes too much urine.
  • Swallowing problems: anencephaly, esophageal atresia/TEF, duodenal atresia
  • Excess urine: maternal diabetes (osmotic diuresis)
  • Others: multiple gestation, alloimmunization/hydrops, TTTS recipient
  • Oligohydramnios: post-term, PUV, renal agenesis, NSAIDs, placental insufficiency, ROM
exam_pearl: Three of four options here are oligohydramnios causes; anencephaly is the swallowing-defect odd one out.

stem: A 30-year-old PG at 30 weeks of gestation with severe preeclampsia complaining of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: RUQ or epigastric pain in "severe preeclampsia" comes from the liver: hepatic edema, periportal hemorrhage or subcapsular hematoma stretch the liver (Glisson) capsule. The pain is itself a severe feature and should prompt checking for HELLP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Esophagitis gives retrosternal burning related to reflux; it is not part of preeclampsia pathophysiology.
B. Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised lipase; it would be the answer with gallstones or alcohol, not as the mechanism of preeclamptic pain.
C. Gastric ulcer causes meal-related epigastric pain (NSAIDs, H. pylori) and is unrelated to preeclampsia.
key_concept:
Preeclampsia + RUQ/epigastric pain = liver capsule distension.
  • It is a severe feature of preeclampsia
  • Check platelets, liver enzymes, hemolysis (HELLP)
  • Hepatic rupture: rare catastrophic complication with shock
exam_pearl: In a hypertensive third-trimester patient, RUQ pain is the liver, not the stomach or gallbladder, until proven otherwise.

stem: A 28-year-old G4 P3 AO at 12 weeks of gestation with a prior history of preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction presented to the Antenatal Clinic. Which of the following will most likely reduce the risk of growth restriction and preeclampsia?
why_right: A prior history of preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction makes her high risk for recurrence, and she is at 12 weeks, the ideal time to start prophylaxis. Low-dose aspirin started before 16 weeks and continued to about 36 weeks reduces the risk of preeclampsia and placenta-related growth restriction.
why_wrong_block:
B. Progesterone prevents preterm birth in women with a short cervix or previous spontaneous preterm birth; it does not prevent preeclampsia or FGR.
C. Multivitamins have no proven effect on preeclampsia or growth restriction risk.
D. Ferrous sulfate prevents or treats iron deficiency anemia; it does not change placental disease risk.
key_concept:
High-risk woman for preeclampsia = low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks (before 16 weeks) until about 36 weeks.
  • High-risk features: previous preeclampsia, chronic HTN, pregestational diabetes, CKD, autoimmune disease (SLE, APS)
  • Aspirin: prevents preeclampsia and FGR
  • Progesterone: prevents preterm birth (short cervix, prior preterm birth)
  • Folic acid: prevents neural tube defects
  • Iron: prevents anemia
exam_pearl: Match the prophylaxis to the problem: placenta (preeclampsia/FGR) = aspirin; cervix/preterm birth = progesterone or cerclage.

stem: A 23-year-old primigravida presents to the Emergency Room at 35 weeks of gestation complaining of decreased fetal movement for the last few hours. Examination revealed the cervix is 1 cm dilated and the head is at -2 station. Cardiotocography shows that the baseline is 160 beats per minute with good accelerations, good variability, and early decelerations. The uterine contractions are mild and regular. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: good accelerations, good variability, and early decelerations
why_right: The CTG is reassuring: baseline 160 (upper limit of normal), good accelerations, good variability and early decelerations (benign). However, regular contractions with a cervix 1 cm dilated at 35 weeks suggest preterm labor, so she should stay for observation with continuous CTG monitoring rather than go home.
why_wrong_block:
A. Discharge fits decreased fetal movement with a reassuring CTG and no labor (kick chart); here regular contractions and cervical change mean possible preterm labor.
B. Cesarean section needs fetal distress or an obstetric indication; this CTG is reassuring.
C. Augmentation is for established active-phase labor with inadequate contractions; it would be wrong to accelerate a preterm labor at 1 cm.
key_concept:
Decreased fetal movement plus contractions changes the plan.
  • Reassuring CTG, no labor: discharge with kick chart
  • Reassuring CTG, regular contractions + cervical change: admit and continuous CTG
  • Early decels: head compression, benign
  • Baseline 110 to 160 is normal
exam_pearl: Same reassuring CTG, but regular contractions with a dilated cervix turn "discharge" into "observe".

stem: A 30-year-old GS P3013 woman presented in labor at term. She had a vaginal delivery complicated by abruption placenta. She was then noted to have significant uterine bleeding. The team in charge noted she had bleeding from multiple venipuncture sites. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
why_right: Placental abruption is a classic trigger of DIC, and bleeding from multiple venipuncture sites shows a systemic coagulopathy, not just a uterine problem. Diffuse coagulopathic bleeding will not stop with mechanical or surgical measures, so the best next step is to correct the coagulopathy with blood products, then continue medical management, before any surgical step.
why_wrong_block:
B. Internal iliac ligation is a surgical step after medical failure; operating on an uncorrected DIC patient will not stop the oozing.
C. Uterine packing (tamponade) treats bleeding from the placental bed; it cannot stop diffuse bleeding that also comes from venipuncture sites.
D. The B-Lynch compression suture is for atony at laparotomy; it is not the first step when bleeding is due to DIC.
key_concept:
PPH: identify the T before choosing the step.
  • Bleeding from IV sites or gums = coagulopathy (Thrombin)
  • Obstetric DIC triggers: abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, IUFD, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, sepsis
  • Order: correct coagulopathy, then medical, then surgical
exam_pearl: Venipuncture-site bleeding flips the answer from a uterine procedure to coagulopathy correction.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presented at full term at labor, she was having uncontrolled diabetes during this pregnancy. Which of the following neonatal complications will most likely increase?
why_right: Uncontrolled maternal diabetes causes fetal hyperglycemia and compensatory fetal hyperinsulinemia; insulin inhibits surfactant production and lung maturation, so the infant of a diabetic mother has an increased risk of respiratory distress syndrome, even at term.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fetal hyperinsulinemia persists after the maternal glucose supply is cut at birth, causing neonatal hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia.
B. Chronic fetal hypoxia stimulates erythropoiesis, so these babies are polycythemic (high hemoglobin), not anemic.
C. Fetal hypoxia raises erythropoietin levels, which is what drives the polycythemia.
key_concept:
Infant of a diabetic mother: everything goes in the opposite direction to the distractors.
  • Respiratory distress syndrome (insulin blocks surfactant)
  • Hypoglycemia (hyperinsulinemia)
  • Polycythemia, high erythropoietin, hyperbilirubinemia
  • Macrosomia, shoulder dystocia
  • Hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia
  • Congenital anomalies (pregestational), e.g. caudal regression, cardiac defects
exam_pearl: Diabetic mother = baby hypoglycemic and polycythemic, never hyperglycemic or anemic.

stem: A 30-year-old, 12 weeks pregnant woman presented to the Emergency Room with vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed her fundal height corresponded with 19 weeks of gestation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clue is a uterus far larger than dates: "12 weeks pregnant" but "fundal height corresponded with 19 weeks", together with first trimester "vaginal bleeding". Uterine enlargement beyond gestational age with bleeding is the classic picture of a complete mole, where the cavity fills with hydropic villi and blood clot and the beta-hCG is very high.
why_wrong_block:
A. Partial mole classically gives a uterus normal or small for dates (often with a growth restricted fetus); marked enlargement points to a complete mole instead.
C. Threatened abortion is bleeding with a closed os and a viable fetus whose size matches the dates; the uterus is not 7 weeks larger than expected.
D. Abdominal pregnancy is extrauterine, so it does not enlarge the uterus beyond dates; suspect it with abdominal pain, easily felt fetal parts and an empty uterus on imaging.
key_concept:
First trimester bleeding + uterus large for dates = complete mole until proven otherwise.
  • Complete mole: uterus large for dates, no fetus, snowstorm or cluster of grapes on ultrasound, very high beta-hCG.
  • Partial mole: uterus normal or small for dates, fetal parts present, focal cystic placental change.
  • Threatened abortion: closed os, viable fetus, size equals dates.
  • Confirm with ultrasound plus serum beta-hCG.
exam_pearl: Size greater than dates favours complete mole; size equal to or less than dates with a fetus favours partial mole.

stem: A 24-year-old primigravida presents at 12 weeks gestation to an antenatal visit. Blood electrolytes and renal function tests were requested 3 days earlier. Which of the following is the most expected finding on her blood tests?
OptA: A fall in serum creatinine level
OptB: An increase of plasma sodium level
OptC: Increased plasma blood urea nitrogen level
OptD: Unaffected serum blood urea nitrogen level
why_right: At "12 weeks gestation" renal plasma flow and GFR have already risen substantially, increasing creatinine clearance. Filtration of creatinine therefore rises and serum creatinine falls (by about 0.3 mg/dL, mostly by 20 weeks), which is the most expected finding on routine renal tests in normal pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Plasma sodium does not increase; fluid retention and plasma volume expansion cause a small dilutional FALL of about 2 to 4 mEq/L.
C. BUN does not increase in normal pregnancy; the higher GFR lowers it by about half in the first trimester. A raised BUN suggests dehydration or renal impairment.
D. BUN is not unaffected; it falls in the first trimester for the same reason creatinine falls (raised GFR).
key_concept:
Normal pregnancy: GFR up, so filtered waste products go down.
  • Creatinine clearance: up about 40 to 50% by 16 weeks
  • Serum creatinine: down about 0.3 mg/dL
  • BUN: down about 50% in the first trimester
  • Sodium: down 2 to 4 mEq/L (dilution)
  • Uric acid: down early, rises toward term
  • Urine protein: up to about 300 mg/day can be normal
exam_pearl: A "normal" nonpregnant creatinine in pregnancy may actually reflect renal impairment.

stem: A 30-year-old Primigravida is found to have hyperthyroidism during her pregnancy. Which of the following is the most contraindicated?
why_right: The question asks for the most contraindicated treatment in a pregnant woman with hyperthyroidism. Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated: it crosses the placenta and is taken up by the fetal thyroid (from roughly 10 to 12 weeks), ablating it and causing fetal hypothyroidism. Every other option is usable in pregnancy in the right setting.
why_wrong_block:
A. Propranolol is used short term for adrenergic symptom control (palpitations, tremor) while antithyroid drugs take effect.
B. Methimazole is avoided in the first trimester (PTU preferred then) but is the drug of choice in the second and third trimesters; it is not absolutely contraindicated.
C. Thyroidectomy is an accepted option, best in the second trimester, when drugs fail, are not tolerated or there is a compressive goiter.
key_concept:
Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy: drugs by trimester, RAI never.
  • 1st trimester: PTU (methimazole embryopathy risk)
  • 2nd/3rd trimester: switch to methimazole (PTU hepatotoxicity)
  • Beta-blocker: short-term symptom control
  • Surgery: second trimester if drugs fail
  • Radioactive iodine: absolutely contraindicated (fetal thyroid ablation)
exam_pearl: Methimazole is only 'relatively' avoided (1st trimester); radioactive iodine is the absolute contraindication.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with unusual vaginal bleeding and a fleshy vaginal mass. She underwent a suction evacuation for hydatidiform mole. Her beta-hCG level was 870,000 mIU/mL prior to the procedure. She was followed with weekly beta-hCG levels for 5 weeks, with the following results: 1st week: 576 mIU/mL 2nd week: 350 mIU/mL 3rd week: 180 mIU/mL 4th week: 70 mIU/mL 5th week: 300 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptC: Perform a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
OptD: Perform a metastatic workup without biopsy
why_right: After molar evacuation hCG fell to 70 and then rose to 300, with "unusual vaginal bleeding" and a "fleshy vaginal mass": this is post-molar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, most likely choriocarcinoma with a vaginal metastasis. The diagnosis is made clinically from the hCG trend, so the next step is metastatic workup and staging without biopsy before choosing chemotherapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Continued surveillance fits a steadily falling hCG; a rise plus a vaginal mass is neoplasia and needs action now.
B. Chemotherapy is the treatment, but the regimen depends on stage and risk score, so staging must come first.
C. Biopsy is not needed because the diagnosis rests on hCG and the clinical picture, and these highly vascular lesions can bleed catastrophically.
key_concept:
Post-molar GTN sequence: rising or plateaued hCG, clinical diagnosis, staging, then chemotherapy.
  • Diagnosis: hCG plateau or rise after evacuation (no histology needed)
  • Common metastatic sites: lungs, vagina, liver, brain
  • Workup: pelvic imaging, chest imaging, plus CT/MRI as indicated
  • Low risk: single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin D
  • High risk: multi-agent chemotherapy
exam_pearl: A fleshy, friable vaginal or cervical mass after a pregnancy is a metastasis: never biopsy it.

stem: A pregnant lady at term presented at labor and delivered a healthy child with 3.5 kilogram. After that, the placenta didn't deliver and she is starting to bleed a large amount of blood What's the best drug to give her for her postpartum hemorrhage?
highlight_terms_source: bleed a large amount of blood
why_right: She has heavy bleeding with a retained placenta, so she needs a uterotonic to contract the uterus. Oxytocin is first line but is not offered; misoprostol (a prostaglandin E1 analogue) is the only uterotonic among the choices. Definitive treatment of the retained placenta is still manual removal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Propofol is an anesthetic induction agent; it may be used for anesthesia during manual removal but does nothing to stop the bleeding.
C. Nifedipine is a tocolytic and antihypertensive; relaxing the uterus would worsen atonic bleeding. It is right for preterm labor or severe hypertension in pregnancy.
D. Magnesium sulfate relaxes smooth muscle and can worsen atony; it is right for eclampsia prevention or fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks.
key_concept:
Uterotonic choice in PPH.
  • Oxytocin: first line
  • Methylergonovine: avoid in hypertension
  • Carboprost: avoid in asthma
  • Misoprostol: useful when others unavailable; the only uterotonic in this list
  • Tranexamic acid: adjunct within 3 hours of birth
  • Tocolytics (nifedipine, MgSO4, terbutaline) relax the uterus: never for PPH
exam_pearl: If oxytocin is missing from the options, pick the only remaining uterotonic and reject anything that relaxes the uterus.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is seen in the infertility clinic as a case of primary infertility for 2 years. Her history revealed that she has had amenorrhea for the last 6 months and only gets menstruation through using withdrawal bleeding pills. She had investigations repeated twice, performed 3 months apart, and they were all showing the same results. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: only gets menstruation through using withdrawal bleeding pills
investigations repeated twice, performed 3 months apart
why_right: Secondary amenorrhea for 6 months in a 25-year-old who bleeds only with withdrawal pills, with the same results on labs "repeated twice, 3 months apart", is the setting of confirmed premature ovarian insufficiency (high FSH/LH, low estrogen). The failed ovary has no responsive follicles, so the priority is hormone replacement therapy to replace estrogen, protect bone and the cardiovascular system and relieve vasomotor symptoms. Pregnancy, if desired, would require donor oocytes rather than ovulation induction.
why_wrong_block:
A. GnRH acts on the pituitary to release FSH/LH, but in POI gonadotropins are already high and the defect is in the ovary; GnRH is useful in hypothalamic amenorrhea, not here.
C. Clomiphene works by raising endogenous FSH; in POI FSH is already elevated and the ovary cannot respond. It suits normogonadotropic anovulation such as PCOS.
D. Exogenous gonadotropins cannot stimulate a follicle-depleted ovary; they are used in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or clomiphene-resistant PCOS.
key_concept:
POI (under 40) = amenorrhea + raised FSH on repeat testing + low estrogen; treat with HRT, fertility via egg donation.
  • Confirm with repeat FSH weeks apart (stem: repeated, same result)
  • HRT: bone protection, vasomotor relief, cardiovascular protection
  • Ovulation induction (Clomid, gonadotropins, GnRH) is futile
  • Fertility option: donor oocyte IVF
exam_pearl: Repeated labs unchanged + bleeds only on withdrawal pills = ovarian failure: replace hormones, do not try to stimulate the ovary.

stem: long case, female only gets period when using withdrawal or something pills, Labs (sorry don't remember numbers i just compared them to reference they put in the q stem) high FSH, low porgesterone, normal TSH or thyroxine, LH normal, Estradiol or estrogen normal, next step or best management (i don't remember) options:
OptD: Clomid ? (not clomiphene literally, but something similar, maybe its generic name)
highlight_terms_source: only gets period when using withdrawal
why_right: She bleeds only with withdrawal pills (no spontaneous cycles) and has a high FSH with low progesterone and normal TSH: this is premature ovarian insufficiency, where the ovary itself has failed and the pituitary is already driving it hard. The best management is hormone replacement therapy, which replaces the missing ovarian hormones to protect bone and the cardiovascular system and relieve vasomotor symptoms. Stimulating ovulation is futile because there are no responsive follicles left.
why_wrong_block:
A. GnRH injection acts on the pituitary to release FSH/LH; here FSH is already high, so the problem is ovarian, not hypothalamic. Pulsatile GnRH is right for hypothalamic amenorrhea (LOW FSH and LH).
B. Gonadotropin ovulation induction needs ovaries that can respond; a failed ovary with high endogenous FSH will not. Right for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or clomiphene-resistant PCOS.
D. Clomiphene works by raising the patient's own FSH, which is already high here, so it adds nothing. Right for anovulatory PCOS (normal FSH) wanting pregnancy.
key_concept:
Amenorrhea: read the FSH first; high FSH = ovarian failure, so replace hormones rather than stimulate.
  • High FSH (± LH), low estrogen/progesterone = POI: HRT; fertility via egg donation
  • Low FSH and LH = hypothalamic/pituitary cause: pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins
  • Normal FSH, anovulation (PCOS) wanting pregnancy: clomiphene/letrozole
  • Confirm POI with a repeat raised FSH weeks apart; consider karyotype (Turner)
exam_pearl: High FSH means the ovary is the problem: any ovulation induction option is a trap; HRT is the answer.

stem: female 12 week (yes 12 weeks i remember the number) gestation, investigation shows cystic hygroma in fetus, next step or bests way to confirm dx?
why_right: A cystic hygroma at 12 weeks is strongly linked to aneuploidy (Turner syndrome, trisomies), so the fetus needs a karyotype. At 12 weeks the invasive test that can be done now is chorionic villus sampling (window about 10 to 13 weeks), giving an early confirmed diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amniocentesis is done from about 15 weeks (15 to 20 weeks), so it is too early at 12 weeks. It is right if the hygroma or abnormal screen is found in the second trimester.
C. Option not recalled. Likely distractors: termination (premature before a karyotype confirms the diagnosis) or fetal blood sampling (only later in pregnancy and higher risk).
key_concept:
Invasive prenatal diagnosis is chosen by gestational age.
  • CVS: 10 to 13 weeks
  • Amniocentesis: 15 to 20 weeks
  • Fetal (umbilical) blood sampling: later second trimester onward
  • Cystic hygroma: think Turner (45,X) and trisomies: karyotype
exam_pearl: The gestational age in the stem picks the test: 12 weeks = CVS, 16 weeks = amniocentesis.

stem: A 39-year-old G4 P3 at 12 weeks of gestation came for an ultrasound study. Ultrasound: Single viable fetus with cystic hygroma. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management to be offered at this gestational age?
why_right: A cystic hygroma on a first trimester scan carries a high risk of aneuploidy (Turner syndrome, trisomies), so fetal karyotyping is the next step. The lead-in asks what can be offered "at this gestational age": at 12 weeks the only invasive test in its window is chorionic villus sampling (10 to 13 weeks). It gives an early diagnosis on which further decisions can be based.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amniocentesis is done from 15 to 20 weeks, so it is too early at 12 weeks. It would be right if the hygroma were found at 16 weeks.
C. Termination before any confirmed diagnosis is premature; some fetuses with a hygroma have a normal karyotype. It is only discussed after the karyotype and counselling.
D. Cordocentesis (PUBS) is a later, higher risk procedure, used from about 18 to 20 weeks, for example for fetal anemia or a rapid karyotype late in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Invasive prenatal diagnosis is chosen by gestational age.
  • CVS: 10 to 13 weeks
  • Amniocentesis: 15 to 20 weeks
  • Cordocentesis: about 18 to 20 weeks onward
  • Cystic hygroma or raised nuchal translucency at the first trimester scan = offer karyotype
exam_pearl: Same scenario at 16 weeks flips the answer to amniocentesis; read the gestational age first.

stem: A 23-year-old patient at 38 weeks of gestation is in active labor and diagnosed with cord prolapse. Which of the following is the most expected finding on CTG?
why_right: A prolapsed cord is compressed between the presenting part and the pelvis, and umbilical cord compression produces variable decelerations. Sustained compression cuts off fetal blood flow and causes sudden, prolonged fetal bradycardia, which is the classic CTG picture of cord prolapse.
why_wrong_block:
A. Accelerations are a reassuring sign of fetal wellbeing; they are not expected when the cord is being compressed.
B. Late decelerations reflect uteroplacental insufficiency (e.g. pre-eclampsia, IUGR, hyperstimulation), not cord compression.
C. Early decelerations come from fetal head compression and are benign; they mirror the contractions and are typical once the head is engaged.
key_concept:
Match the deceleration to its cause.
  • Early: head compression, mirror image of contraction, benign
  • Variable: cord compression (cord prolapse, oligohydramnios), abrupt and variable in timing
  • Late: uteroplacental insufficiency, start after the contraction peak, ominous
  • Cord prolapse: variable decelerations + bradycardia; relieve pressure and deliver by emergency cesarean
exam_pearl: Cord = variable; head = early; placenta = late.

stem: Abd. Pain, anorexia and abd. Distension.... Bilateral ovarian cancer... CA125 90(normal 30) Wt Type of cancer?
key_concept:
Ovarian tumor type follows age and marker. A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to epithelial ovarian tumor.
  • CA-125: epithelial (most common, older women, often bilateral serous)
  • AFP, beta-hCG, LDH: germ cell (young women)
  • Inhibin: granulosa cell (sex cord stromal)
  • Y chromosome dysgenetic gonad: gonadoblastoma
exam_pearl: Raised CA-125 + ascites + bilateral masses in an adult = epithelial ovarian cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of loss of appetite, bloating and abdominal pain. Clinical assessment and investigations confirmed the presence of moderate ascites, pleural effusion and bilateral ovarian masses. Cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) was 95 unit/ml. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 45-year-old with bloating, anorexia, ascites, pleural effusion and bilateral ovarian masses plus a raised CA-125 has advanced epithelial ovarian cancer. CA-125 is the marker of epithelial tumors, which are the most common ovarian cancers, occur in older women, are often bilateral (serous type) and present late with ascites.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sex cord stromal tumors present with hormonal effects (estrogen excess bleeding, virilization) and use inhibin as a marker, not CA-125. Choose it for postmenopausal bleeding with a solid mass or raised inhibin.
B. Germ cell tumors affect young women with a usually unilateral, rapidly growing mass and raised AFP, beta-hCG or LDH.
D. Gonadoblastoma arises in dysgenetic gonads carrying Y chromosome material in young patients; nothing here suggests that.
key_concept:
Ovarian mass: age and tumor marker point to the type.
  • Epithelial: older women, CA-125, ascites, often bilateral
  • Germ cell: young, AFP / beta-hCG / LDH
  • Granulosa (sex cord stromal): inhibin, estrogen effects
  • Diagnosis confirmed by histopathology; staging is surgical
exam_pearl: Ascites + pleural effusion with a benign solid ovarian fibroma is Meigs syndrome, but with raised CA-125 and bilateral masses think epithelial cancer.

stem: Ovarian cyst with fatty material:
key_concept:
Fatty cyst content = dermoid. A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst).
  • Dermoid: fat, sebum, hair, teeth; risk of torsion
  • Granulosa cell tumor: solid, estrogen, inhibin
  • Thecoma: solid, estrogen
  • Fibroma: solid, Meigs syndrome
exam_pearl: Fibroma, thecoma and granulosa cell tumor are solid, so they never leak fatty contents.

stem: A 30-year-old woman underwent ovarian cystectomy. While the nurse was preparing the specimen to be sent to histopathology, there was a leak of thick fatty material from the cyst. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: leak of thick fatty material from the cyst
why_right: The clue is the content: "thick fatty material" leaking from an ovarian cyst. A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is a germ cell tumor containing skin derivatives, so it is filled with sebaceous, fatty material and often hair and teeth. It is the most common benign ovarian tumor in women of reproductive age, fitting a 30-year-old.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fibroma is a solid sex cord stromal tumor of older women (linked to Meigs syndrome); being solid, it has no fatty fluid to leak.
B. Thecoma is a solid, estrogen-secreting stromal tumor, usually postmenopausal, presenting with abnormal bleeding; it is not cystic.
D. Granulosa cell tumor is a mostly solid, estrogen-secreting tumor (Call-Exner bodies) causing bleeding or precocious puberty; it does not contain sebaceous material.
key_concept:
Ovarian tumor by content:
  • Sebum, fat, hair, teeth: mature cystic teratoma (dermoid)
  • Chocolate-colored old blood: endometrioma
  • Solid, Meigs syndrome: fibroma
  • Solid, estrogen effects: thecoma, granulosa cell tumor
  • Dermoid complication: torsion (heavy, mobile cyst)
exam_pearl: Fatty or hairy contents = dermoid; the sex cord stromal tumors in the options are all solid.

stem: Female Patient complaining of dysmenorrhea which is interfer in evaluation of history
why_right: In a woman with dysmenorrhea, the menstrual history is the most important part of the evaluation: age at onset relative to menarche, timing of pain in the cycle, duration, cycle regularity, flow and associated symptoms. These details separate primary dysmenorrhea (starts within 1 to 2 years of menarche, no pathology) from secondary dysmenorrhea (later onset, progressive, with heavy bleeding, dyspareunia or infertility).
why_wrong_block:
A. Family history adds supporting clues (e.g. endometriosis in relatives) but does not define the type of dysmenorrhea. It leads when the question is about hereditary risk.
C. Medical history matters for drug choice (e.g. NSAID contraindications) but does not characterise the pain.
D. Surgical history is relevant for adhesions or prior pelvic surgery but is secondary to the menstrual pattern.
key_concept:
Dysmenorrhea workup starts with the menstrual history.
  • Primary: onset within 1 to 2 years of menarche, normal exam, crampy pain at start of menses
  • Secondary: later onset (often >25 years), progressive, abnormal exam
  • Red flags for secondary: heavy bleeding, dyspareunia, infertility, enlarged or fixed uterus
exam_pearl: Timing of onset relative to menarche is the single detail that splits primary from secondary dysmenorrhea.

stem: A 37-week pregnant woman came for ECV (External Cephalic Version). Which factor affects the result / what is the most important thing to confirm before ECV?
highlight_terms_source: most important thing to confirm before ECV
why_right: A non-reassuring fetal monitoring pattern is a contraindication to ECV, so a CTG must be done before ECV to confirm fetal wellbeing, and it is repeated afterwards to detect fetal compromise (bradycardia, cord or placental problems) caused by the manoeuvre. A reassuring pre-procedure CTG is therefore the key thing to confirm before attempting version at 37 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prolonged maternal fasting is not a requirement for ECV and does not affect its success; the procedure is done with facilities for emergency delivery available, not after a set fast.
B. Gestational age is already established at 37 weeks; ultrasound before ECV is used to confirm breech presentation, placental site and liquor volume, not to re-date the pregnancy.
key_concept:
ECV: offer from about 37 weeks; check fetal wellbeing and exclude contraindications first.
  • Before: ultrasound to confirm presentation, placenta and liquor; reassuring CTG
  • After: repeat CTG; anti-D if Rh negative
  • Contraindications: placenta previa, non-reassuring CTG, significant third trimester bleeding, multiple pregnancy, uterine malformation, oligohydramnios / liquor abnormality, IUGR, major fetal anomaly
exam_pearl: A CTG with variable decelerations before ECV converts the plan into a contraindication.

stem: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks gestation — which vaccine should be given?
why_right: Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for all pregnant women at any gestational age, including 30 weeks, because influenza causes more severe disease in pregnancy and maternal antibodies protect the newborn. It is not a live vaccine, so it is safe in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Varicella is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy; give it before conception or postpartum to a non-immune woman.
B. MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy; give it preconception (then avoid pregnancy for a period) or postpartum to a rubella non-immune woman.
key_concept:
Pregnancy vaccines: inactivated yes, live no.
  • Give in pregnancy: inactivated influenza (any trimester), Tdap (late second to third trimester)
  • Avoid in pregnancy: MMR, varicella, other live vaccines
  • Live vaccines: preconception or postpartum
exam_pearl: If Tdap appears among the options at this gestation it competes with influenza; with only live vaccines as alternatives, influenza is the answer.

stem: A 23-year-old primigravida presented at 31 weeks of gestation with preterm labor. Examination revealed, the uterus is contracting and the cervix is closed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is magnesium sulfate because at 31 weeks (below 32 weeks) a woman in preterm labor is given MgSO4 for fetal neuroprotection, reducing the risk of cerebral palsy if she delivers. The listed alternatives are tocolytics only and none of them protects the fetal brain. MgSO4 is not chosen for its tocolytic effect, which is weak and not recommended for that purpose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nifedipine is a first-line tocolytic that can buy time for steroids, but it gives no fetal neuroprotection, which this key prioritizes below 32 weeks.
B. Terbutaline is a beta mimetic with significant maternal side effects (tachycardia, pulmonary edema); it is not first line and has no neuroprotective effect.
C. Indomethacin is a tocolytic option before 32 weeks, but it risks fetal ductus constriction and oligohydramnios and gives no neuroprotection.
key_concept:
Preterm labor drug ladder by gestation.
  • Below 32 weeks: MgSO4 for neuroprotection
  • Below 34 weeks: antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity (priority if asked for a single drug)
  • Tocolysis (nifedipine, atosiban; indomethacin below 32 weeks) to allow steroids to work
  • GBS prophylaxis antibiotics if delivery expected
exam_pearl: If corticosteroids are among the options below 34 weeks, they take priority over MgSO4.

stem: Q: pain two day before and during the cycle on NSAID
highlight_terms_source: pain two day before and during the cycle
why_right: Pain starting two days before and during menses is dysmenorrhea, and the key clue is that she is already on an NSAID and still has pain. In primary dysmenorrhea, NSAID failure means moving to hormonal therapy with combined oral contraceptive pills, which suppress ovulation and thin the endometrium, lowering prostaglandin release.
why_wrong_block: B. A copper IUD worsens dysmenorrhea and bleeding; the levonorgestrel IUS can help but is not the usual next step after NSAID failure. An IUD fits a woman needing long-acting contraception, not this stepwise pain question.
key_concept:
Primary dysmenorrhea ladder.
  • Step 1: lifestyle (heat, exercise)
  • Step 2: NSAIDs (first-line drug)
  • Step 3: NSAID failure: combined OCP
  • Still failing or red flags: look for secondary cause (endometriosis), laparoscopy
exam_pearl: Not yet on NSAIDs = NSAIDs; already on NSAIDs with persistent pain = OCP.

stem: A 20-year-old primigravida presented at 31 weeks of gestation with a headache and blurred vision. Urine examination by dipstick shows ++ proteinuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: New proteinuria (dipstick ++) after 20 weeks (31 weeks) in a primigravida with headache and blurred vision is pre-eclampsia. The CNS symptoms are severe features, making this pre-eclampsia with severe features.
why_wrong_block:
B. Primary renal disease would usually be known before pregnancy or show proteinuria before 20 weeks, and does not explain new headache and visual symptoms.
C. Pyelonephritis presents with fever, flank pain, rigors and pyuria, not headache and blurred vision.
D. Chronic hypertension starts before pregnancy or before 20 weeks and by itself does not cause new proteinuria with CNS symptoms (that would be superimposed pre-eclampsia).
key_concept:
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are classified by timing and end-organ involvement.
  • Chronic: before 20 weeks or pre-pregnancy
  • Gestational: after 20 weeks, no proteinuria or end-organ damage
  • Pre-eclampsia: after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction
  • Severe features: headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, BP ≥160/110, HELLP labs
  • Eclampsia: pre-eclampsia plus seizures
exam_pearl: Headache or visual symptoms upgrade pre-eclampsia to severe: think MgSO4 and IV antihypertensive next.

stem: A 23-year-old primigravida is admitted for induction of labor at term. On examination, the cervix is closed and 3.5 cm long. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to be given for cervical ripening?
highlight_terms_source: cervix is closed and 3.5 cm long
why_right: A cervix that is closed and 3.5 cm long is uneffaced and undilated, so the Bishop score is low (unfavorable). Induction will likely fail unless the cervix is ripened first, and vaginal prostaglandin E₂ (dinoprostone) is the standard pharmacological ripening agent before oxytocin or amniotomy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methergine (methylergometrine) is an ergot uterotonic used to treat postpartum hemorrhage from atony; it causes tetanic contraction and is never used with a fetus in utero.
B. Methyldopa is an antihypertensive for chronic or gestational hypertension in pregnancy; it has no effect on the cervix.
C. Vaginal progesterone maintains cervical length and is used to prevent preterm birth in women with a short cervix; it does the opposite of ripening.
key_concept:
Unfavorable cervix (low Bishop score) → ripen first; favorable cervix → oxytocin ± amniotomy.
  • Bishop score: dilation, effacement, station, consistency, position
  • Pharmacological ripening: prostaglandin E₂ (vaginal), misoprostol (PGE₁)
  • Mechanical ripening: Foley balloon catheter
  • Favorable cervix: amniotomy + oxytocin infusion
exam_pearl: Oxytocin is not a ripening agent; giving it to a closed, long cervix is the classic wrong answer for failed induction.

stem: pregnant with placenta (Not sure abruption/previa) Postpartum bleeding.. how to prevent it in next pregnancy? (I don't remember the options but i tried)
key_concept:
Previous PPH or placental bleeding = high risk in the next pregnancy: plan, prepare, deliver in the right place.
  • Painless bleeding = previa; painful bleeding = abruption
  • Previa: TVUS localization, no vaginal exam, cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
  • Abruption risk factors: hypertension, smoking, trauma
  • Prophylaxis at delivery: active management of the third stage (oxytocin)
  • Deliver in a unit with blood bank and theatre access
exam_pearl: After placental bleeding or a previous PPH, the next pregnancy is high risk: the answer is always about planning and preparing, never simple reassurance.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presented with crampy, lower abdominal pain beginning with the onset of menses every month, and lasting for 2 to 3 days. There was no pain between menses, but reported radiation of pain to the lower back and upper thighs, along with nausea, fatigue, and headache which has been present for several years and progressively getting worse. Physical examination normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: beginning with the onset of menses
why_right: A 19-year-old with crampy pain that begins with the onset of menses and lasts 2 to 3 days, radiating to the back and thighs with nausea, fatigue and headache, and a normal examination, is the textbook picture of primary dysmenorrhea: prostaglandin-mediated pain with no pelvic pathology.
why_wrong_block:
A. Secondary dysmenorrhea is pain from pelvic pathology (endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID); suspect it with onset later in life, pain outside menses, dyspareunia or abnormal findings, none of which are present.
B. Premenstrual syndrome starts in the luteal phase, days before menses, and resolves early in menstruation; here the pain starts with menses and there is no pain beforehand.
D. Endometriosis gives secondary dysmenorrhea, often with dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, infertility or nodularity and a fixed uterus on exam; the exam here is normal and the timing is confined to menses.
key_concept:
Pain timing + exam decides dysmenorrhea type.
  • Primary: young, starts with menses, 1 to 3 days, normal exam → NSAIDs, then COCP
  • Secondary: older onset, pelvic pathology, abnormal exam → ultrasound, treat cause
  • PMS: luteal-phase symptoms that ease once menses begins
  • Worsening pain over years is a reason to reassess for secondary causes, but with a normal exam and classic timing the diagnosis stays primary
exam_pearl: Symptoms before menses = PMS; pain starting with menses + normal exam = primary dysmenorrhea.

stem: A 44-year-old woman (P5005) presents to the clinic with an uncomfortable sensation in the vagina for the last year. She reports pelvic pressure associated with urinary frequency but no urinary leaks or irregular menstruation. Obstetric history includes 5 term spontaneous vaginal deliveries. She works in loading and unloading heavy boxes. Examination reveals a large bulging of the anterior vaginal wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: large bulging of the anterior vaginal wall
why_right: Pelvic pressure with "urinary frequency" and "a large bulging of the anterior vaginal wall" is a symptomatic cystocele. She is 44 and medically free, the defect is large and symptomatic, and her heavy lifting job makes conservative measures unlikely to succeed, so she is a surgical candidate and the repair is anterior colporrhaphy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kegel exercises are conservative therapy for small or asymptomatic prolapse and first line for stress incontinence; they will not correct a large symptomatic cystocele.
B. Vaginal pessary is chosen for elderly or comorbid women who are unfit for or decline surgery; she is young and healthy.
C. Bladder suspension (colposuspension/sling) treats stress urinary incontinence; she explicitly has "no urinary leaks".
key_concept:
Prolapse management fork:
  • Conservative (pessary, pelvic floor exercises): small defect, asymptomatic, or comorbid unfit for surgery
  • Surgery: large defect, symptomatic, healthy woman
  • Cystocele: anterior colporrhaphy; rectocele: posterior colporrhaphy
  • Cystocele: check post-void residual and urinalysis (UTI risk)
  • Leakage present: think sling/TVT, not prolapse repair alone
exam_pearl: Same cystocele in an elderly diabetic with heart failure flips the answer to a pessary.

stem: A 42-year-old P3003 healthy woman presents with heavy prolonged vaginal bleeding over the past 7 months. Her periods have become longer and progressively heavier, with the last one occurring 15 days ago. Pelvic examination reveals a small amount of blood in the vaginal vault, normal-sized uterus, and mobile ovaries. (See reports.) Pelvic ultrasound: Endometrium 13 mm and a 2.2 cm x 1 cm lesion in the uterine cavity. Endometrial biopsy: Normal histology. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Magnetic resonance imaging of the uterus
OptD: Evaluate hemoglobin level and coagulopathy screening
highlight_terms_source: 2.2 cm x 1 cm lesion in the uterine cavity
why_right: Ultrasound shows a focal 2.2 x 1 cm intracavitary lesion, but the blind endometrial biopsy was normal. A biopsy samples only part of the cavity and can miss a focal lesion, so the lesion must still be characterized: saline infusion sonohysterogram outlines polyps versus submucous fibroids and guides hysteroscopic removal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Examination under anesthesia does not image the uterine cavity; it is used for assessing pelvic or cervical pathology, not a focal intracavitary lesion.
C. MRI is costly and not first line for a focal cavity lesion; it is reserved for mapping complex fibroids or suspected adenomyosis when ultrasound is inconclusive.
D. Coagulation screening is for heavy bleeding since menarche or without a structural cause; here a structural lesion has already been found in a healthy woman.
key_concept:
Normal blind biopsy does not exclude a focal intracavitary lesion.
  • AUB >45 yr: endometrial biopsy
  • Focal lesion on TVUS: sonohysterogram
  • Then hysteroscopy for diagnosis and removal
  • Coagulopathy screen: heavy bleeding since menarche, no structural cause
exam_pearl: Focal lesion on US + normal biopsy = sonohysterogram, not reassurance.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is scheduled to undergo a myomectomy due to the presence of a large uterine fibroid. The surgeon is planning to administer medication that will help reduce the size of the uterine fibroid prior to performing the procedure. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to use for this purpose?
highlight_terms_source: reduce the size of the uterine fibroid
why_right: The goal is to reduce the size of a large fibroid before myomectomy. GnRH agonists create a temporary hypoestrogenic state that shrinks fibroids and reduces bleeding, and they also allow anemia to be corrected before surgery. They are used short term (usually a few months) because of menopausal side effects and bone loss.
why_wrong_block:
B. Combined pills can control fibroid bleeding but do not shrink the fibroid; they fit symptom control in a small symptomatic fibroid.
C. An IUD (even a levonorgestrel one) may reduce bleeding but does not shrink the fibroid, and a large fibroid distorting the cavity makes insertion and retention unreliable.
D. Progestogens may reduce bleeding but do not reliably shrink fibroids, and some fibroids grow under progesterone.
key_concept:
Fibroid drug choice depends on the goal.
  • Shrink before surgery: GnRH agonist
  • Control bleeding symptoms: OCP, NSAIDs, tranexamic acid
  • Preop GnRH also stops bleeding so anemia can be corrected
  • GnRH limited to short courses: hot flushes, bone loss
exam_pearl: "Reduce the size" = GnRH; "control the bleeding" = OCP or other medical therapy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0144).

stem: A 20-year-old woman presented with a history of primary infertility for 1 year. She had a history of scanty irregular cycles with prolonged intervals (see lab results). Which of the following is the important workup?
highlight_terms_source: scanty irregular cycles with prolonged intervals
why_right: The labs are not reproduced in this recall, but the intended picture is premature ovarian insufficiency: a 20-year-old with scanty, irregular, widely spaced cycles and labs showing high FSH and LH with low estradiol. Ovarian failure this young needs a karyotype to look for Turner mosaicism or another chromosomal cause, which also guides counselling and screening.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pelvic imaging does not reveal the chromosomal cause of ovarian insufficiency; MRI would be chosen for a structural pelvic question.
B. TSH is part of a general oligomenorrhea screen, but with an ovarian failure lab pattern the important test is karyotype.
C. Hyperprolactinemia gives low or normal FSH/LH, not the high gonadotropins of ovarian failure; choose prolactin if galactorrhea or low gonadotropins are shown.
key_concept:
Read the gonadotropins in oligo/amenorrhea:
  • High FSH/LH, low estradiol, young: ovarian insufficiency, karyotype
  • Low or normal FSH/LH + high prolactin: hyperprolactinemia, then pituitary MRI
  • LH:FSH raised, androgens high: PCOS
  • Always exclude pregnancy and check TSH
exam_pearl: Young woman with high FSH = karyotype; low FSH with high prolactin = pituitary.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is complaining of severe abdominal pain. She is a known case of primary infertility and underwent embryo transfer 3 weeks ago (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: She had "embryo transfer 3 weeks ago" for infertility and now has "severe abdominal pain"; the labs would show a positive beta hCG. Assisted reproduction (IVF, embryo transfer) and the tubal disease that often underlies infertility are recognised risk factors for ectopic (including heterotopic) pregnancy. Pregnancy plus severe pain after IVF is ectopic until proven otherwise.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ovarian torsion: ovarian stimulation can enlarge the ovaries and predispose to torsion, so it is a real differential, but a positive pregnancy test after embryo transfer with severe pain points first to ectopic. Torsion fits sudden unilateral pain with vomiting and an adnexal mass.
C. Acute appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with fever and anorexia; it has no link to embryo transfer and does not explain a positive hCG.
D. Intestinal obstruction: colicky pain with vomiting, distension and absolute constipation, usually after prior surgery or hernia; nothing in this stem suggests it.
key_concept:
Severe abdominal pain in early pregnancy: exclude ectopic first.
  • Risk factors: IVF/embryo transfer, previous ectopic, PID or tubal surgery, IUD in situ, smoking
  • IVF also raises risk of heterotopic pregnancy (intrauterine + ectopic)
  • Work up: beta hCG + transvaginal ultrasound
  • Unstable: surgery; stable and small: methotrexate or expectant per criteria
exam_pearl: An intrauterine pregnancy on scan after IVF does not fully exclude ectopic: heterotopic pregnancy is more likely after assisted reproduction.

stem: A 36-year-old presented to the Antenatal Clinic for an Ultrasound scan. Ultrasound: Single viable fetus with significant increased levels of amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: Polyhydramnios results from either reduced fetal swallowing or increased fetal urine output. In anencephaly the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid normally, so fluid accumulates. It is the only option that raises fluid; the other three all cause oligohydramnios.
why_wrong_block:
B. Post-term pregnancy is linked to declining placental function and oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios.
C. Posterior urethral valves obstruct fetal urine outflow, reducing amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios).
D. Maternal NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin) reduce fetal renal output and cause oligohydramnios; indomethacin is even used therapeutically to reduce fluid.
key_concept:
Polyhydramnios = fetus cannot swallow, or makes too much urine.
  • Swallowing problems: anencephaly, esophageal atresia/TEF, duodenal atresia
  • Excess urine: maternal diabetes (osmotic diuresis)
  • Others: multiple gestation, alloimmunization/hydrops, TTTS recipient
  • Oligohydramnios: post-term, PUV, renal agenesis, NSAIDs, placental insufficiency, ROM
exam_pearl: Three of four options here are oligohydramnios causes; anencephaly is the swallowing-defect odd one out.

stem: A 28-year-old Primigravida presented to the Antenatal Clinic for an Ultrasound scan. Ultrasound: Single viable fetus with significant lower levels of amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: Amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy is mainly fetal urine, so oligohydramnios means reduced fetal urine output, membrane rupture or a urinary tract problem. Placental insufficiency reduces fetal renal perfusion, so the fetus makes less urine and fluid falls. It is the only option on the list that lowers fluid.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chorioangioma (placental vascular tumor) is associated with polyhydramnios, not oligohydramnios.
B. Duodenal atresia impairs fetal swallowing and absorption, so fluid accumulates and causes polyhydramnios.
C. Uncontrolled maternal diabetes causes fetal hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis, giving polyhydramnios.
key_concept:
Amniotic fluid = fetal urine in, fetal swallowing out.
  • Oligohydramnios: uteroplacental insufficiency, rupture of membranes, renal agenesis (Potter), GU obstruction (PUV), NSAIDs, post-term
  • Polyhydramnios: maternal diabetes, multiple gestation, alloimmunization, impaired swallowing (duodenal/esophageal atresia, TEF, anencephaly)
  • TTTS: recipient polyhydramnios, donor oligohydramnios
exam_pearl: Less urine OUT (kidneys, placenta, leak) = oligo; less swallowing IN or more urine (diabetes) = poly.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Companion 'Q:' question under 1997 (oligohydramnios counterpart).

stem: A 23-year-old pregnant woman presented with frequency and dysuria for 5 days (see lab result), Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 76 /min, Temperature 37.6 °C. Test Result Normal Values: Leukocytes 30 0-3 per high power field. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
why_right: A pregnant woman with frequency and dysuria, pyuria (leukocytes 30/hpf) and only a low-grade temperature (37.6 °C) with normal vitals has acute cystitis, not pyelonephritis. The recall's key is Augmentin (amoxicillin clavulanate) because a beta-lactam is safe throughout pregnancy and covers the usual urinary organisms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Flucloxacillin is an anti-staphylococcal penicillin for skin and soft tissue infections; it has poor activity against E. coli and other urinary gram-negatives.
C. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone avoided in pregnancy because of concerns about fetal cartilage toxicity.
D. Nitrofurantoin is widely used for cystitis in pregnancy but is avoided near term because of neonatal hemolysis risk; this source treats it as second to a beta-lactam when one is offered.
key_concept:
UTI or asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy: always treat, with pregnancy-safe agents, then send a test of cure.
  • Safe: amoxicillin or Augmentin, cephalexin, nitrofurantoin (not near term)
  • Avoid: fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines
  • Trimethoprim: avoid in the first trimester (folate antagonist)
  • Fever, flank pain, vomiting = pyelonephritis → admit for IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: When a beta-lactam is listed for cystitis in pregnancy, SMLE keys usually prefer it over nitrofurantoin.

stem: A 59-year-old woman undergoes a hysteroscopy secondary to her complain of abnormal uterine bleeding for the last couple of months (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 59-year-old (postmenopausal) woman with abnormal uterine bleeding whose hysteroscopy shows a smooth, soft, vascular mass projecting into the cavity has an endometrial polyp. Polyps are focal endometrial overgrowths that hysteroscopy both confirms and removes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adenomyosis is endometrium within the myometrium, giving a diffusely enlarged, tender uterus with dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia; it is not seen as a mass inside the cavity at hysteroscopy.
B. Endometriosis is endometrial tissue outside the uterus (ovaries, pelvic peritoneum), diagnosed by laparoscopy, not hysteroscopy, and it usually regresses after menopause.
C. A subserosal fibroid grows toward the outer surface of the uterus, causing pressure symptoms rather than bleeding, and is invisible from inside the cavity; a submucosal fibroid would be the intracavitary fibroid.
key_concept:
Intracavitary lesion seen at hysteroscopy = polyp or submucosal fibroid.
  • Polyp: soft, vascular, often pedunculated → hysteroscopic polypectomy and histology
  • Submucosal fibroid: firm, pale, smooth → AUB, infertility
  • Subserosal fibroid: outer surface → pressure symptoms
  • Adenomyosis: diffuse globular tender uterus
  • Postmenopausal bleeding always needs endometrial assessment to exclude cancer
exam_pearl: A blind endometrial biopsy can miss a polyp; hysteroscopy is the test that sees and removes it.

stem: Pregnant woman developed DIC associated with obstetric complication. Most likely cause?
why_right: Among obstetric complications, placental abruption is the most common cause of DIC in pregnancy. Separation of the placenta releases large amounts of tissue factor (thromboplastin) from the retroplacental clot into the maternal circulation, triggering consumptive coagulopathy, especially with large or concealed abruptions.
why_wrong_block: A. Placenta previa causes painless, often heavy bleeding from the lower segment, but it does not release thromboplastin, so DIC arises only secondarily after massive hemorrhage and transfusion.
key_concept:
Obstetric causes of DIC: abruption first.
  • Placental abruption (most common)
  • Amniotic fluid embolism
  • Severe pre-eclampsia or HELLP
  • Retained dead fetus
  • Sepsis, massive PPH
exam_pearl: Painful bleeding + coagulopathy (oozing from IV sites, low fibrinogen) = abruption until proven otherwise.

stem: year-old G4P2 woman with previous postpartum hemorrhage is currently pregnant and worried about recurrence. Strongest risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage?
key_concept:
PPH risk factors (atony is the most common cause):
  • Maternal: grand multiparity, previous PPH
  • Fetal: macrosomia, multiple gestation, polyhydramnios
  • Labor: prolonged or precipitous labor, induction or augmentation
  • Pick the factor the stem actually gives (parity, weight, number of babies, history)
exam_pearl: In PPH risk-factor questions, read the numbers in the stem (parity, labor length, birth weight, number of fetuses, past history) before choosing.
