stem: A pregnant woman G7P6 gave birth after labor of 7 hours had post-partum hemorrhage, what was her most likely risk factor?
why_right: She is G7P6, a grand multipara, and her labor of 7 hours is neither prolonged nor precipitous. Grand multiparity predisposes to uterine atony, the most common cause of PPH, so it is her most likely risk factor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prolonged labor causes atony from myometrial fatigue, but 7 hours is a normal labor length; the answer would be prolonged labor if the stem gave, for example, 16 hours.
B. Precipitous labor (delivery within about 3 hours of onset) is also a PPH risk factor, but 7 hours is not precipitous.
key_concept:
Match the PPH risk factor to the number in the stem.
  • Para more than 4 with normal labor → grand multiparity
  • Very long labor → prolonged labor
  • Delivery within about 3 hours → precipitous labor
  • Baby above 4000 g → macrosomia
  • Twins → multiple gestation
exam_pearl: A normal labor duration in the stem is placed there to rule out the labor-related options.

stem: 28-week pregnant female with increased vaginal discharge for 6 hours. Sterile speculum showed pooling of fluid in posterior fornix. No contractions. Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: pooling of fluid in posterior fornix
why_right: At 28 weeks, a sudden increase in watery discharge for 6 hours with pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix on sterile speculum examination is diagnostic of rupture of membranes. With no contractions and gestation under 37 weeks, this is preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM).
why_wrong_block:
A. Bacterial vaginosis gives a thin gray discharge with a fishy odor, pH above 4.5 and clue cells, not a pool of amniotic fluid in the fornix.
B. Candidiasis gives a thick white, cottage cheese discharge with itching and normal pH, not watery pooling.
C. Normal secretions in pregnancy increase but are thin and white without pooling; fluid collecting in the posterior fornix is pathological until proven otherwise.
key_concept:
Suspected ROM: sterile speculum first; avoid digital examination.
  • Pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix confirms ROM
  • Supporting tests: nitrazine (alkaline), ferning, IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1, ultrasound for liquor volume
  • PROM ≥37 weeks; PPROM <37 weeks
  • PPROM care: steroids, latency antibiotics (erythromycin), monitor for chorioamnionitis
exam_pearl: No digital vaginal exam in PPROM: it raises infection risk and shortens latency.

stem: 60y Postmenopausal woman with stage IA endometrial cancer. Best treatment?
why_right: Endometrial cancer is staged and treated surgically: total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (with surgical staging) is the primary treatment. Stage IA means the tumour is confined to the uterus with less than half myometrial invasion, so surgery alone is usually curative. A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman has no fertility to preserve, so there is no reason to choose a non-surgical option.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy is for advanced, metastatic or recurrent endometrial cancer; it has no primary role in disease confined to the uterus.
B. Radiotherapy is adjuvant after surgery when there are high-risk features, or primary treatment when the patient is medically unfit for surgery; neither is stated here.
C. Progesterone is the fertility-sparing option for a young woman with low-grade early disease, or for a patient unfit for surgery; she is postmenopausal and not described as unfit.
key_concept:
Endometrial cancer: surgery first (TAH + BSO with staging), then adjuvant therapy by risk.
  • Early, fit patient: hysterectomy + BSO
  • High-risk features after surgery: adjuvant radiotherapy
  • Advanced/metastatic: chemotherapy
  • Young, wants fertility, low grade: progestin with close follow-up
  • Unfit for surgery: progestin or primary radiotherapy
exam_pearl: Progesterone becomes the answer only when the stem adds 'wants fertility' or 'unfit for surgery'.

stem: Stage IIB cervical cancer. Best treatment?
key_concept:
Cervical cancer: stage decides surgery versus chemoradiation.
  • CIN / CIS: excision (LEEP or cone)
  • IA1: cone (fertility) or simple hysterectomy
  • IA2 to IB, early IIA: radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymphadenectomy
  • IIB and above (parametrial spread): concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation
  • Biopsy-proven invasion: stage first, then treat
exam_pearl: Parametrial involvement (IIB) is the line where surgery stops and chemoradiation starts.

stem: Pregnant woman wants to quit smoking but failed previous attempts and is worried about continuing smoking during pregnancy. Most appropriate management?
why_right: Nicotine replacement therapy is first-line pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation. In pregnancy, behavioural support is tried first, but this woman has failed previous attempts and is still smoking, so NRT is offered: it delivers nicotine without the carbon monoxide and other toxins in smoke, so the benefit of quitting outweighs the nicotine exposure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Non-nicotine gum has no pharmacological effect on withdrawal or craving; it is not an evidence-based cessation treatment.
C. Bupropion is not first line and has limited safety data in pregnancy; it also lowers the seizure threshold (contraindicated in epilepsy and eating disorders). It is used outside pregnancy when NRT fails or is declined.
key_concept:
Smoking cessation ladder.
  • All smokers: brief advice + behavioural support
  • First-line drug: NRT (patch + short-acting form)
  • Second line: varenicline
  • Bupropion: avoid in epilepsy, eating disorders
  • Pregnancy: counselling first; NRT if counselling fails; avoid varenicline and bupropion
exam_pearl: 'Pregnant + failed quitting with counselling' points to NRT, never varenicline or bupropion.

stem: 45-year-old woman with endometriosis failed medical therapy and does not desire future fertility. Most definitive management?
why_right: The definitive treatment of endometriosis is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, because removing the ovaries removes the estrogen that drives the ectopic implants. It is chosen for refractory disease (failed medical therapy) in a woman who has completed her family, which fits this 45-year-old exactly.
why_wrong_block:
B. Laparoscopic ablation/excision of lesions is the first surgical step and preserves fertility, but implants recur; it is not the definitive option for a woman who does not want more children.
C. Endometrial ablation destroys the uterine lining to treat heavy menstrual bleeding; it does not touch ectopic endometrial implants in the pelvis.
D. Combined OCP is first-line medical therapy; medical therapy has already failed here.
key_concept:
Endometriosis treatment ladder.
  • NSAIDs for pain
  • First-line hormonal: combined OCP or progestin
  • Second line: progestin-releasing IUD (or GnRH agonist)
  • Medical failure: laparoscopic ablation/excision (fertility-sparing)
  • Definitive, family complete: TAH + BSO
exam_pearl: 'Most definitive' plus 'no future fertility' means removing uterus AND ovaries, not just ablating lesions.

stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 34? Weeks Was admitted 10 days ago for observation due to headache, seizures and drowsiness? presents with headache and BP 140/92 mmHg. She has no seizures. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: This woman has already had seizures and drowsiness in this pregnancy (eclampsia) and now has a headache, a severe feature, with raised BP at 34 weeks. Magnesium sulfate is the drug that prevents (and treats) eclamptic seizures and is mandatory with severe features; at 34 weeks it is given alongside planning delivery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are teratogenic (fetal renal damage) and are contraindicated in pregnancy.
B. Labetalol is the first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy (started from about 140/90 in pre-eclampsia, urgently at ≥160/110), but it only lowers BP and does not prevent seizures; after eclamptic symptoms the priority is seizure prophylaxis.
key_concept:
Pre-eclampsia with severe features / eclampsia.
  • ABC, then MgSO4 for seizures
  • Severe BP (≥160/110): IV labetalol or hydralazine
  • Deliver at ≥34 weeks, or earlier if deteriorating
  • Steroids if delivery expected before 34 weeks
  • Never ACE inhibitors/ARBs in pregnancy
exam_pearl: Antihypertensives treat the number; only magnesium sulfate protects the brain from seizures.

stem: Which vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy?
why_right: Oral polio vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine, and live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy because of the theoretical risk of fetal infection. It is the only live vaccine among the options; if a pregnant woman needs polio protection, inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) is preferred.
why_wrong_block:
B. Diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccines are inactivated toxoids/acellular antigens; the adult form (Tdap) is actually recommended in every pregnancy in the third trimester.
C. Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for all pregnant women at any gestational age; only the live intranasal form is avoided.
key_concept:
Vaccines in pregnancy: live = avoid, inactivated = allowed.
  • Avoid (live): MMR/rubella, varicella, live zoster, OPV, BCG, yellow fever (unless high risk)
  • Recommended: inactivated influenza (any trimester), Tdap (third trimester)
  • Allowed if indicated: hepatitis B, IPV
  • Not live but deferred: HPV
  • Rubella/varicella: give before pregnancy to non-immune women
exam_pearl: Spot the live vaccine; 'oral' polio is live, 'inactivated' polio is not.

stem: A woman with BMI of 35 and PCOS, presents with her athlete healthy husband to the clinic with 2 years of failure to conceive. What should you do?
OptB: Do tests for her husband and tell her to eat healthy
key_concept:
Infertility (≥12 months, or ≥6 months if the woman is 35 or older): investigate the couple.
  • Male: semen analysis first; if abnormal, FSH, LH, testosterone
  • Female: ovulation (cycle history, mid-luteal progesterone), then tubal patency (HSG)
  • PCOS + obesity: weight loss first, then letrozole/clomiphene
  • A known female cause never skips the male workup
exam_pearl: A 'healthy athlete' husband is a distractor: appearance never replaces a semen analysis.

stem: elderly around 70s or 60s female pt, complain of vaginal bleeding, us show thickining endometrial wall 18 mm, pt unfit for surgery.
why_right: Postmenopausal bleeding with an 18 mm endometrium means hyperplasia or cancer until proven otherwise. The standard treatment would be hysterectomy, but she is unfit for surgery, so progestin therapy (continuous oral progesterone) is the best alternative to suppress the endometrium. In practice an endometrial biopsy is obtained first to confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy is for advanced or metastatic endometrial cancer, not for a thickened endometrium or premalignant hyperplasia.
B. Radiotherapy is used for proven endometrial cancer (adjuvant, or primary when inoperable); it is not the treatment for hyperplasia and nothing here confirms cancer.
C. Observation is unsafe: postmenopausal bleeding with an endometrium well above the 4 to 5 mm cut-off carries a real risk of hyperplasia with atypia or cancer.
key_concept:
Postmenopausal bleeding: TVUS, then biopsy if the endometrium is thickened.
  • Hyperplasia without atypia: progestin
  • Atypia, fit, no fertility wish: hysterectomy
  • Atypia, young wanting fertility: progestin + follow-up biopsy
  • Atypia or early cancer, unfit for surgery: continuous progestin (oral or LNG-IUD)
exam_pearl: 'Unfit for surgery' is the clue that turns hysterectomy into progesterone.

stem: A female had molar pregnancy two years ago. What's the prediction for her current pregnancy?
OptA: She's gonna have the same incidence as of normal other pregnancies,
why_right: This recall's key is contraception because the source's teaching is that pregnancy should be deferred with reliable contraception after a molar pregnancy until hCG follow-up is complete, so that a rising hCG from persistent trophoblastic disease is not confused with a new pregnancy. The broader point is that a past mole changes how a later pregnancy is handled.
why_wrong_block: A. Wrong because the risk of another molar pregnancy is increased after one mole (around 1%, clearly above the general population), so a later pregnancy is not 'the same as normal'; it needs an early ultrasound and an hCG check after it ends.
key_concept:
After a molar pregnancy.
  • Serial hCG until normal, then a period of monitoring
  • Reliable contraception during follow-up (hormonal contraception is acceptable)
  • Recurrence risk about 1% after one mole, higher after two
  • Next pregnancy: early ultrasound; hCG after delivery or loss
  • Rising or plateauing hCG: gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
exam_pearl: Contraception matters during hCG surveillance; years later the issue is increased recurrence risk, not avoidance of pregnancy.

stem: 35 years old, female, been married for three years. She was trying to conceive for 18 months, didn't get pregnant. What is the best next step?
OptB: test her and her husband for infertility
why_right: Infertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (6 months if the woman is 35 or older). She has been trying for 18 months at 35, so she clearly qualifies, and the next step is investigation of both partners: semen analysis for the husband and ovulation and tubal assessment for her.
why_wrong_block: A. IVF is a treatment for a specific diagnosis (e.g. bilateral tubal blockage, severe male factor, or failed simpler treatments); it is never started before the couple has been investigated.
key_concept:
When to investigate infertility.
  • Under 35: after 12 months of trying
  • 35 or older: after 6 months
  • Under the threshold: reassure, continue trying
  • Workup: semen analysis first, then ovulation, then HSG for tubes
  • Treatment (ovulation induction, IVF) only after a diagnosis
exam_pearl: Investigation always precedes treatment; IVF is never the first step.

stem: 23-year-old newly married female with irregular menstrual cycles is seeking contraception. She prefers to avoid methods that require daily use. Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive option?
highlight_terms_source: avoid methods that require daily use
why_right: The decisive clue is that she "prefers to avoid methods that require daily use". The contraceptive transdermal patch is changed once a week, so it gives reliable hormonal contraception without a daily pill, and like the combined pill it also tends to regulate her irregular cycles. A young, healthy, newly married woman has no stated contraindication to estrogen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Combined oral contraceptive pills: would regulate her cycle and is the usual choice for a young woman with menstrual complaints, but it must be taken every day, which she wants to avoid.
B. Condom: has to be used at every act of intercourse, has a higher typical use failure rate and does nothing for her irregular cycles; it is chosen mainly for STI protection.
C. Diaphragm: also needs action at every intercourse, is less effective than hormonal methods and has no effect on cycle irregularity.
key_concept:
Match the method to the stated preference: no daily dosing = weekly patch, monthly ring, 3-monthly injection or LARC (IUD/implant).
  • Daily: combined pill, progestogen-only pill
  • Weekly: combined transdermal patch
  • Monthly: vaginal ring (estrogen + progestogen)
  • Every 3 months: Depo-Provera
  • Per act: condom, diaphragm, spermicide
  • Combined hormonal methods also regulate cycles and relieve menorrhagia/dysmenorrhea
exam_pearl: The contraceptive patch delivers estrogen PLUS a progestogen; if the same stem says she is happy with a daily pill, the key flips to the combined oral pill.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A 'Q:' block follows (screenshot on next page) with a different variant: newly married with dysmenorrhagia and heavy menstrual bleeding, answer Combined oral (see 2128b).

stem: Female newly married w.. Has dysmenorrhagia and heavy menstrual bleeding.. Want to use contraception.. What is appropriait?
why_right: A newly married woman who wants contraception and has dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding is best served by one method that treats all three problems. The combined oral contraceptive gives reliable contraception, reduces menstrual blood loss, relieves dysmenorrhea and regulates the cycle, and nothing in the stem contraindicates estrogen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mirena (levonorgestrel IUD): very effective for heavy bleeding and is a first-line option for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, but this recall keys the pill for a young, newly married woman; Mirena is favoured when estrogen is contraindicated or long-acting reversible contraception is preferred.
B. Progestogen-only pill: less effective and commonly causes irregular bleeding, so it does not control heavy menses; it is chosen when estrogen is contraindicated (breastfeeding, VTE risk, cardiac disease).
key_concept:
Contraception wanted + menorrhagia/dysmenorrhea in a healthy young woman = combined OCP.
  • Breastfeeding or under 6 weeks postpartum: avoid estrogen, use progestogen-only methods
  • VTE, cardiac disease or anticoagulated: progestogen-only or IUD
  • Chronic heavy menstrual bleeding options: LNG-IUD (Mirena) or COCP
  • NSAIDs help dysmenorrhea but are not contraceptive
exam_pearl: Add an estrogen contraindication (smoker over 35, migraine with aura, VTE, breastfeeding) and the answer moves to Mirena or a progestogen-only method.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown under the 'Q:' label of 2128 (printed as '2- ...'); answer line in screenshot: 'Combined oral'.

stem: 17y, pregnant primigravida 9 weeks, complain mild vaginal bleeding, US: crown rump length 9 weeks and heartbeat +. Next step?
highlight_terms_source: crown rump length 9 weeks and heartbeat +
why_right: Bleeding in early pregnancy is assessed with both transvaginal ultrasound and pelvic examination before the type of abortion can be named. The ultrasound already shows a viable 9-week intrauterine pregnancy, so the next step is pelvic (speculum) examination to check whether the cervical os is open or closed, look for products of conception and exclude a local cervical or vaginal cause of bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV progesterone: progesterone is not given intravenously and is not started before the abortion type is established by examination.
C. Ultrasound for placental position: placental localization matters for bleeding after 20 weeks (placenta previa), not at 9 weeks, and an ultrasound has already been done.
D. Reassurance and expectant management: this is the management once the examination confirms a closed os (threatened abortion); it comes after the pelvic examination, not instead of it.
key_concept:
First trimester bleeding: history + pelvic exam + TVUS, then classify, then treat.
  • Closed os, viable fetus: threatened, reassurance and outpatient follow up
  • Open os, products still inside: inevitable/incomplete, evacuation
  • Closed os, nonviable fetus, no bleeding history: missed, evacuation or medical management
  • Closed os, uterus empty, products passed: complete
  • Bleeding after 20 weeks: localize placenta BEFORE any digital exam
exam_pearl: If the stem already reports a closed os on examination, the answer flips to reassurance and expectant management.

stem: Treatment of yellowish vaginal discharge with itching?
why_right: Yellowish (yellow-green, often frothy and offensive) discharge with itching is the pattern of trichomoniasis, caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. Treatment is oral metronidazole, and the sexual partner must be treated at the same time.
why_wrong_block: B. Clotrimazole: a topical azole for vulvovaginal candidiasis, which gives thick white cottage-cheese odorless discharge with intense itching and pseudohyphae; it has no activity against Trichomonas.
key_concept:
Vaginal discharge: colour + smell + microscopy picks the drug.
  • Trichomonas: yellow-green frothy, strawberry cervix, motile flagellates, metronidazole + treat partner
  • Bacterial vaginosis: grey thin fishy, clue cells, pH above 4.5, metronidazole (partner not treated)
  • Candida: white curdy odorless, pseudohyphae, normal pH, azoles
  • Gonorrhea: purulent, Gram-negative diplococci, ceftriaxone + partner
  • Chlamydia: purulent, azithromycin/doxycycline + partner
exam_pearl: Change "yellowish" to "white cottage-cheese, odorless" and the answer becomes clotrimazole.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 38 kg/m²) and chronic hypertension is planning pregnancy. She is concerned about the risk of intrauterine fetal demise. Which of the following preconception interventions is most important for reducing this risk?
why_right: Both obesity (BMI 38) and chronic hypertension are independent risk factors for intrauterine fetal demise: hypertension reduces uteroplacental perfusion (growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, abruption), while obesity adds risk through placental dysfunction, gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia. Since she has both, preconception care should target both together, so neither single intervention is the whole answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Optimal blood pressure control alone: essential (switch to pregnancy-safe agents and reach target BP), but it leaves the separate stillbirth risk of her obesity untreated.
B. Weight reduction alone: lowers risk of stillbirth, gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia, but uncontrolled hypertension would still threaten placental perfusion.
D. Smoking cessation: a real stillbirth risk factor through placental vasospasm, but she is not described as a smoker, so it does not address her actual risks (this option was not fully recalled).
key_concept:
Preconception care = optimise every modifiable risk factor the patient actually has.
  • Chronic hypertension: control BP, change to pregnancy-safe drugs (stop ACE inhibitors/ARBs)
  • Obesity: weight loss before conception, higher-dose folic acid, early glucose screening
  • Smoking: cessation (vasospasm, growth restriction, abortion)
  • Diabetes: tight glycaemic control before conception
  • All women: folic acid started before conception
exam_pearl: When the stem lists two independent modifiable risk factors and offers "both", the exam usually wants both addressed.

stem: Patient in her 30s with PCOS and oligomenorrhoea has hirstium what is the best investigation for hirsitum
why_right: In a woman with known PCOS and hirsutism, serum testosterone is the test used to document and quantify hyperandrogenism, so it is the best investigation for her hirsutism. It also screens for an androgen-secreting tumour, suspected when the level is markedly raised.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sex hormone binding globulin: usually low in PCOS and used with testosterone to calculate the free androgen index, but it is not the primary test for hirsutism.
C. 17-hydroxyprogesterone: screens for non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which mimics PCOS; it is chosen when CAH is suspected, not to assess hirsutism in established PCOS.
D. Prolactin: part of the workup of oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea to exclude hyperprolactinemia, but it does not measure androgen excess.
key_concept:
PCOS = 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on US.
  • Hirsutism: serum testosterone
  • Typical finding: raised LH relative to FSH (about 3:1)
  • Once suspected: glucose tolerance and lipid profile
  • Exclude mimics: TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP (CAH)
  • Rapid virilization or very high testosterone/DHEAS: look for a tumour
exam_pearl: If the question asks to EXCLUDE late-onset CAH as the cause of hirsutism, the answer becomes 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

stem: Women complains of irregular menses with facial hair but no signs of virilism, what to do to prevent such condition?
OptB: do screening for PCOs and testosterone level
key_concept:
Hirsutism + irregular menses: confirm PCOS and exclude mimics first, then treat and screen metabolically.
  • No virilization (clitoromegaly, deep voice, rapid onset) = benign cause such as PCOS likely
  • Virilization or very high testosterone: exclude ovarian/adrenal tumour
  • Workup: testosterone, LH:FSH, TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP, pelvic US
  • After diagnosis: glucose tolerance and lipid profile
  • Treatment: lifestyle first, COCP for cycles/hirsutism, metformin for insulin resistance
exam_pearl: The words "no virilism" lower suspicion of a tumour; they do not by themselves establish PCOS.

stem:
A 20-year-old woman presented to the Maternal Health Clinic with severe facial acne and irregular menstrual bleeding. Examination shows fine hair growth on the chin, upper back. breasts and lower abdomen. A pregnancy test is returned negative. She returns to the clinic on the 5th day of her menstrual cycle and has a serum sample drawn for analysis (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values
Follicle-stimulating hormone 10 5-20 IU/L
Luteinizing hormone 28 5-22 U/L
Prolactin 890 < 870 pmol/L
Testosterone 3.2 0.7-2.8 mol/L
Which additional laboratory values should be obtained?
OptA: Thyroid stimulating hormone and free T3 and T4
why_right: Severe acne, irregular bleeding, hirsutism, a raised LH (28) relative to FSH (10) and a raised testosterone (3.2) establish PCOS; the prolactin is only marginally above range. Once PCOS is diagnosed, the additional tests needed are a glucose tolerance test and lipid profile, because PCOS carries insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia risk that must be screened.
why_wrong_block:
A. TSH with free T3 and T4: thyroid disease is a mimic to exclude in irregular menses, but the diagnosis here is already PCOS and the needed tests are metabolic; a full thyroid panel is chosen only with thyroid symptoms or abnormal TSH.
B. Progesterone and TSH: a mid-luteal progesterone confirms ovulation (infertility workup), but anovulation is already evident from the irregular cycles and adds nothing here.
C. DHEA and androstenedione (printed as "androstenolone"): these look for an adrenal androgen source, appropriate with rapid virilization or very high androgens; this picture is ovarian PCOS.
key_concept:
PCOS confirmed: screen the metabolic complications.
  • Glucose tolerance test (insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes)
  • Lipid profile (dyslipidemia, cardiovascular risk)
  • LH:FSH about 3:1 supports PCOS
  • Testosterone: test for hirsutism
  • Long term: endometrial hyperplasia risk from unopposed estrogen
exam_pearl: Asked "which test assesses her hirsutism" the answer is testosterone; asked "which additional labs" after PCOS is clear, it is glucose and lipids.

stem: Patient post partum distressed sob desaturated i think. Has +ve homan test What is the appropriate test for the preliminary diagnosis?
key_concept:
Suspected DVT: pretest probability picks the first test.
  • Low probability: D-dimer; negative excludes, positive leads to compression ultrasound
  • Intermediate or high probability: compression ultrasound first
  • High suspicion, negative ultrasound: D-dimer, then repeat ultrasound in about a week if positive
  • Suspected PE in pregnancy with leg signs: start with leg compression ultrasound
  • Venography: reserved for non-diagnostic ultrasound
exam_pearl: D-dimer only rules out VTE in low-probability patients; pregnancy and postpartum states raise it anyway.

stem: women in vaginal delivery on examination Baby nose orbit mouth and chin felt. What is the next step in management
highlight_terms_source: Baby nose orbit mouth and chin felt
key_concept:
Face presentation: the chin (mentum) decides.
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Monitor partographic progress.
  • Palpable mouth, nose, orbital ridges and chin = face presentation
  • Mentum anterior: trial of vaginal delivery, CS if it fails
  • Mentum posterior: caesarean section
  • Avoid oxytocin augmentation and instrumental rotation
exam_pearl: "Mentum posterior" flips the answer to caesarean; without it, watch the partogram.

stem: A 25-year-old woman G2 P1001 was admitted at 39 weeks' gestation in Labor Suite with labour pains. On Abdominal examination, 3 moderate contractions every 10 minutes. The cervix was 6 cm dilated, 80% effaced. Mouth, lips, nose and orbital hollows were palpable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: Mouth, lips, nose and orbital hollows were palpable
why_right: "Mouth, lips, nose and orbital hollows were palpable" means a face presentation. She is in active labour ("6 cm dilated") with adequate contractions (3 in 10 minutes), and neither fetal distress nor a mentum posterior position is stated. Most face presentations rotate to mentum anterior and can deliver vaginally, so the next step is to monitor partographic progress and intervene only if labour fails.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT pelvimetry does not guide management of a face presentation in active labour; progress on the partogram tests the pelvis.
B. Emergency caesarean section is for persistent mentum posterior, arrest of labour or fetal distress; none is stated here.
C. Oxytocin augmentation is for inadequate contractions with slow progress in a normal presentation; contractions are adequate, and oxytocin in malpresentation risks obstruction and uterine rupture.
key_concept:
Face presentation in labour: manage by mentum position.
  • Palpable mouth, nose, orbits, chin = face
  • Mentum anterior: trial of vaginal delivery, CS if it fails
  • Mentum posterior: caesarean section
  • No oxytocin augmentation in malpresentation
  • Fetal distress or arrest: caesarean at any point
exam_pearl: If the stem adds "mentum posterior", fetal distress or arrest of labour, caesarean becomes right; without these, monitor the partogram.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot variant belonging to 2161 (top of p541); D marked with ** and highlighted.

stem: A 39-year-old woman, who is a mother of 3 children and has completed her family, she is a known case of endometrioma in the right ovary that has been removed 2 years ago. She came to the clinic complaining of mild to moderate dysmenorrhea and deep pain during intercourse along with her chronic lower abdomen pain. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed the presence of left ovarian cyst measuring 6X7 cm that appeared to be an endometriotic cyst. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Removing the cyst when the size becomes more than 10 cm
OptB: Aspiration of the content of cyst under ultrasound guidance
OptC: Total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
OptD: Removing the cyst laparoscopically with ablation of any endometriotic spot
highlight_terms_source: dysmenorrhea and deep pain during intercourse
why_right: A previously excised right endometrioma and now a new "6X7 cm" left endometriotic cyst with dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and chronic pelvic pain means recurrent, symptomatic endometriosis. A symptomatic endometrioma of this size needs surgery, and the first-line surgical step is laparoscopic cystectomy with ablation of endometriotic spots, which relieves pain, lowers recurrence and gives histology. Her symptoms are only "mild to moderate", so radical surgery is not yet justified.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waiting until the cyst exceeds 10 cm leaves a symptomatic endometrioma untreated; she has pain now and is already a surgical candidate.
B. Ultrasound-guided aspiration has a high recurrence rate and gives no tissue diagnosis; it is not a recommended treatment for endometriomas.
C. TAH + BSO is the definitive option for severe or refractory disease after conservative surgery fails in a woman with a completed family; her symptoms are only mild to moderate.
key_concept:
Endometriosis treatment ladder:
  • Initial test: transvaginal ultrasound (ground-glass chocolate cyst)
  • Confirmatory: laparoscopy with biopsy
  • Medical first line: COCP or progestin
  • Surgical first line: laparoscopic cystectomy/ablation
  • Recurrent endometrioma: laparoscopic cystectomy + ablation
  • Definitive: TAH + BSO for refractory severe disease, family complete
exam_pearl: "Completed her family" tempts you to TAH + BSO, but mild to moderate symptoms still get conservative laparoscopic surgery first.

Options: A. Laparoscopic cystectomy and ablation of endometriotic tissue; B. Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy; C. Remove when > 10 mm. stem: A 60-year-old woman presents for a routine gynecology checkup. She is asymptomatic, but an incidental finding of grade 3 posterior vaginal wall prolapse was detected. She denies any symptoms related to urine or stool incontinence. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: incidental finding of grade 3 posterior vaginal wall prolapse
why_right: She is asymptomatic and the prolapse was an incidental finding at a routine checkup, with no bowel or urinary symptoms. Prolapse is treated according to symptoms, not anatomical grade, so even a grade 3 posterior wall prolapse (rectocele) is managed conservatively with reassurance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hysterectomy addresses uterine prolapse and is major surgery; it is not indicated for an asymptomatic posterior wall defect.
B. Posterior repair (posterior colporrhaphy) is the operation for a symptomatic rectocele after failed conservative treatment; this patient has no symptoms.
D. Transvaginal mesh is not indicated for asymptomatic prolapse and carries mesh complications such as erosion and pain.
key_concept:
Prolapse is treated for symptoms, not for grade.
  • Asymptomatic: reassurance and observation
  • Mild symptoms: pelvic floor exercises or pessary
  • Unfit for surgery: pessary
  • Symptomatic, failed conservative, fit: surgery
  • Rectocele: posterior colporrhaphy; cystocele: anterior colporrhaphy
exam_pearl: A high grade does not flip to surgery; symptoms do.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version: 60 yrs asymptomatic, incidental grade 3 posterior wall prolapse not affecting urination or defecation; options A. Hysterectomy, B. Posterior wall repair, C. Conservative management or maybe follow up. Screenshot (0430) Answer: C.

stem: A 32-year-old woman G7 P6 L6 had normal deliveries with no prenatal or postnatal complications. She had an uneventful pregnancy and went into spontaneous vaginal delivery after 7 hours of labor. She delivered a healthy boy weighing 3000 g. After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage?
why_right: "G7 P6 L6" is the decisive clue: six previous births is grand parity (parity >3 in this question set; classically 5 or more births), a maternal risk factor for uterine atony. Her labor length (7 hours) and the baby's weight (3000 g) are both normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. A 7 hour labor is not prolonged.
C. 3000 g is within normal birth weight (2500 to 3500 g).
D. A 7 hour labor is not precipitous; precipitous labor is delivery within about 3 hours of onset.
key_concept:
Uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH; match the stem's numbers to one atony risk factor.
  • Maternal: grand parity (parity >3 in this question set)
  • Fetal: macrosomia (normal birth weight 2500 to 3500 g), multiple gestation
  • Labor: prolonged labor or precipitous labor (delivery within about 3 hours)
  • History: previous PPH
  • Atony on exam: soft, boggy uterus; firm uterus means look for trauma
exam_pearl: Read the P number, not the G number: grand parity is counted by births.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0421 (Answer: A) plus compiler line 'Answer: A. Grand Parity'.

stem: Pregnant 37wks with severe pre eclampsia. The most appropriate step?
why_right: Delivery is the only cure for pre-eclampsia, and with severe pre-eclampsia at 37 weeks (term, well beyond the 34-week threshold) there is nothing to gain by waiting. The plan is immediate delivery after maternal stabilisation with magnesium sulfate and IV antihypertensives, usually by induction of labour.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation (expectant management) is used only for severe pre-eclampsia well before 34 weeks to gain fetal maturity; at 37 weeks it only risks eclampsia, abruption and HELLP.
C. Pre-eclampsia is not by itself an indication for caesarean; delivery is usually by induction of labour, with CS kept for obstetric indications or failed induction.
D. Discharge is never appropriate in severe pre-eclampsia; outpatient care is only for pre-eclampsia without severe features before term.
key_concept:
Pre-eclampsia: gestation and severity decide delivery.
  • Severe features: BP ≥160/110 or end-organ signs (headache, visual change, RUQ pain, low platelets)
  • Severe, ≥34 weeks: stabilise (MgSO4, IV labetalol) then deliver
  • Severe, <34 weeks: admit, steroids, MgSO4, deliver if deteriorating
  • Without severe features, ≥37 weeks: induce labour
  • Mode: vaginal (induction) unless obstetric indication for CS
exam_pearl: "Immediate delivery" means after stabilisation and usually by induction; "prepare for CS" is the trap.

stem: 20-year-old G3 P2002 is in Labor and Delivery Ward in active labor at 6 cm dilatation. The patient is pregnant at 34 weeks and is known to have twin pregnancy. What would be the characteristic that puts this patient at risk of postpartum hemorrhage?
why_right: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage, and over-distension of the uterus by a "twin pregnancy" is a classic fetal-related atony risk factor. Multiple gestation is therefore the characteristic that puts her at risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. Age 20 is not an atony risk factor; advanced maternal age would matter more.
B. Parity 2 (P2002) is below the multiparity threshold of 3 or more that raises atony risk; grand multiparity (5 or more) carries the highest risk.
C. A gestational age of 34 weeks is not itself an atony risk factor; the over-distended uterus from twins is.
key_concept:
Uterine atony risk factors (the 4 Ts: Tone first):
  • Maternal: primigravida, multiparity ≥3
  • Fetal: macrosomia, multiple gestation, polyhydramnios (over-distension)
  • Labour: prolonged or precipitous labour
  • Other causes: trauma (lacerations), tissue (retained placenta), thrombin (DIC)
exam_pearl: Anything that over-stretches the uterus (twins, macrosomia, polyhydramnios) predicts atonic PPH.

stem: 65 post menopause woman complains of insomnia and hot flushes, what is the initial management?
why_right: Hot flushes and insomnia in a postmenopausal woman are vasomotor symptoms, and the initial management is lifestyle modification (cooling measures, layered clothing, avoiding triggers such as caffeine, alcohol and spicy food, weight loss, exercise, sleep hygiene). At "65" she is also beyond the usual window for starting systemic HRT, which strengthens the non-hormonal first step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Soya (phytoestrogen) tablets have inconsistent evidence of benefit and are not a recommended first-line treatment.
C. HRT is second line for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms after lifestyle measures; starting it after age 60 or more than 10 years after menopause carries more cardiovascular and thrombotic risk.
D. Hysterectomy has no role in treating menopausal vasomotor symptoms; it is for uterine pathology such as fibroids or cancer.
key_concept:
Menopausal symptoms: ladder by symptom type.
  • Vasomotor, first line: lifestyle modification
  • Vasomotor, second line: HRT (estrogen + progestogen if uterus intact; estrogen alone after hysterectomy)
  • HRT contraindicated: non-hormonal drugs (SSRI/SNRI, gabapentin)
  • Urogenital (dryness, dyspareunia): topical estrogen
  • Diagnosis: clinical if ≥45 years; FSH if younger
exam_pearl: "Initial" means lifestyle; "most effective" for vasomotor symptoms means HRT.

stem: Post partum women came complaining of headach and tonic clonic seizure. The headach was severe that doesn't relieved by paracetamol, next step ?
why_right: The puerperium is a prothrombotic state, and a postpartum woman with a severe headache not relieved by paracetamol plus a tonic-clonic seizure must be investigated for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Plain CT can miss it, so imaging must include the venous sinuses: CT brain with venography (or MR venography) shows the occluded sinus and guides anticoagulation.
why_wrong_block: A. Non-contrast CT alone excludes haemorrhage and mass but is often normal or nonspecific in venous thrombosis; it fits a first seizure without features suggesting CVST.
key_concept:
Postpartum headache with seizure: think beyond eclampsia.
  • Hypertension ± proteinuria: postpartum eclampsia, give MgSO4
  • Severe refractory headache, seizure, focal signs: CVST, CT or MR venography
  • Thunderclap headache: subarachnoid haemorrhage or reversible vasoconstriction
  • CVST treatment: anticoagulation (LMWH)
exam_pearl: A plain CT can look normal in venous sinus thrombosis; ask for the venogram when the patient is postpartum.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot of same recall: 'Women came after 2 weak postpartm with headache and tonic-clonic seizure, headache not relieved by paracetamol. A-Plan head CT, B-Head ct and venogram. Answer: (B)'.

stem: 19 years old woman came with amenorrhea , no secondary sexual characters low fsh , lh?
OptC: Brain MRI to assess pituitary & hypothalamus
why_right: Primary amenorrhoea at "19" with "no secondary sexual characters" and low FSH and LH is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: the ovaries are not being stimulated because the problem is central. The next step is a brain MRI of the pituitary and hypothalamus to exclude a structural lesion such as a craniopharyngioma or pituitary tumour, after which functional causes (constitutional delay, Kallmann syndrome, low weight or excessive exercise) are considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal/pelvic ultrasound looks for an absent uterus (Mullerian agenesis), which presents with normal breasts and normal gonadotropins; here the problem is central.
B. Starting OCP treats the estrogen deficiency but would skip the work-up; hormone replacement comes after a central lesion is excluded.
key_concept:
Primary amenorrhoea: breasts and FSH sort it.
  • No breasts + high FSH: gonadal failure (Turner), karyotype
  • No breasts + low FSH/LH: central cause, brain MRI
  • Low FSH + anosmia: Kallmann syndrome
  • Breasts present, no uterus: Mullerian agenesis vs androgen insensitivity, ultrasound + karyotype
  • Breasts and uterus present: outflow obstruction (imperforate hymen, transverse septum)
exam_pearl: High FSH sends you to karyotype; low FSH sends you to the brain MRI.

stem: 30 something or late twenties woman complains of secondary amneorrhea for 6 month, normal FSH and prolactin, what is the diagnosis ? ( question had short stem, no labs mentioned)
why_right: Secondary amenorrhea for 6 months with a normal FSH and normal prolactin means the ovary is not failing (FSH would be high) and there is no prolactin cause. With no PCOS option offered, the recall's key places the problem centrally, as dysfunction of the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian (HPO) axis, where gonadotropins sit in the low to normal range. This recall's key is HPO axis failure on that reasoning.
why_wrong_block:
A. Premature ovarian failure is ovarian failure before 40 with high FSH and LH and low estrogen; a normal FSH excludes it. Right when FSH is in the menopausal range in a woman under 40.
B. A vague label that does not name a recognized diagnosis or localize the defect; the lab pattern (normal FSH, normal prolactin) is better described as central HPO axis dysfunction.
key_concept:
Secondary amenorrhea: rule out pregnancy, then read FSH and prolactin.
  • High FSH: premature ovarian insufficiency
  • High prolactin: prolactinoma, drugs, hypothyroidism
  • Normal or low FSH: central (HPO axis) cause such as stress, exercise, weight loss, or PCOS
  • Normal FSH with hyperandrogenism or raised LH:FSH: PCOS
  • Normal hormones after uterine instrumentation: Asherman
exam_pearl: The same stem with PCOS among the options is keyed to PCOS; without it, central HPO axis dysfunction is the intended answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer printed as 'C??' (compiler uncertain).

stem: Pregnant delivered and placenta still in place + 800 cc blood loss , typpe of PPH?
why_right: The bleeding happens right after delivery with the placenta still in place, so it occurs within 24 hours of birth, which defines primary PPH. An 800 mL loss after vaginal birth exceeds the PPH threshold, and timing alone decides the type.
why_wrong_block:
B. Secondary PPH is excessive bleeding from 24 hours up to 12 weeks after delivery, typically from retained tissue or endometritis; here it is immediate.
C. There is no tertiary category; PPH is classified only as primary or secondary.
D. Iatrogenic describes a cause, not a timing category, and nothing in the stem suggests an iatrogenic injury.
key_concept:
PPH is classified by timing.
  • Primary: within 24 hours of delivery (atony, trauma, retained placenta, coagulopathy)
  • Secondary: 24 hours to 12 weeks (retained products, infection)
  • Placenta still in situ with bleeding: think retained or partially separated placenta
exam_pearl: Do not let the undelivered placenta distract you: the question asks the type, and anything within 24 hours is primary.

stem: A pregnant lady, TSH is high, low Free t3 and 4. What to give now?
highlight_terms_source: TSH is high, low Free t3 and 4
why_right: A high TSH with low free T3 and T4 is overt primary hypothyroidism. In pregnancy it must be treated promptly with thyroxine (levothyroxine) because maternal hypothyroidism harms fetal neurodevelopment and raises miscarriage and preterm risk.
why_wrong_block:
B. Propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms of hyperthyroidism; it has no role in an underactive thyroid.
C. Filler option in the recall; not a real choice.
D. Filler option in the recall; not a real choice.
key_concept:
Thyroid labs in pregnancy.
  • High TSH, low fT4: overt hypothyroidism, start levothyroxine
  • Symptomatic hypothyroidism in pregnancy: levothyroxine
  • Low TSH, high fT4: hyperthyroidism, PTU in first trimester then methimazole
  • Monitor TSH and fT4 regularly; thyroxine needs usually rise in pregnancy
exam_pearl: PTU and methimazole are antithyroid drugs for hyperthyroidism; never choose them when TSH is high.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Options printed as 1-4; Answer: 1.
